   We, the undersigned, Al C. Ballard, Mayor of the City of
San Bernardino, State of California, and Jack T. Felton, City
Clerk of said City, do hereby certify and declare as follows:
   The City of San Bernardino, in the County of San Bernar-
dino, State of California, was at all times mentioned herein
and now is a City of the State of California existing and act-
ing under a Charter duly adopted and approved under and
by virtue of Section 8, Article X I of the Constitution of the
State of California, containing a population of over fifty thou-
sand inhabitants.
   The legislative body of said City on its own motion sub-
mitted to the electors of said City, at a Primary Municipal
Election held within said city on the 4th day of February,
1969, certain proposed amendments to the City Charter of said
City._
   Said proposed amendments were published in The San Ber-
nardino Evening Telegram, being a newspaper of general cir-
culation printed and published in said City and having a
general circulation therein, and being an official newspaper of
said City, on the 20th day of December, 1968, in each edition
thereof on said day, and said publication was made at the time
and in the manner prescribed in Section 8, Article X I of the
Constitution of the State of California,
   Said legislative body caused copies of said amendments to
be printed in convenient pamphlet form and in type of not
less than ten-point, and caused copies thereof to be mailed to
each of the qualified electors of said City and, until the day
fixed for said election, advertised in The San Bernardino Eve-
ning Telegram, being a newspaper having a general circulation
in said City, a notice that copies thereof could be had upon
application therefor, and in accordance with said notice copies
thereof could be had upon application therefor.
   Said election was duly and regularly held on the said 4th
day of February, 1969, which said date of the said election
 was not less than forty nor more than sixty days after the
completion of the advertising in said newspaper of said pro-
posed amendments, and at said election a majority of the
qualified voters voting thereon voted in favor thereof and did
ratify said proposed amendments to said City Charter.
   Said proposed amendments were duly and regularly sub-
mitted to, and duly ratified by, the said qualified voters of said
 City, and that all and singular the requirements of the Con-
stitution and laws of the State of California and the Charter
of said City have been complied with.
   Said amendments are as follows:
  Article I I I , Section 33 of the Charter of the City of San
Bernardino is amended to read as follows:
  Section 33. Within fifteen (15) days after its passage, the
City Clerk shall cause each ordinance to be published at least
once in a newspaper of general circulation published and

  Res. Ch. 44]                REGULAR SESSION                 3601

   circulated in the City, or if there is none, or if the charge

  posted in at least three (3) public places in the City. Except
  as otherwise provided in this Charter, an ordinance shall not
  take effect or be valid unless it is published or posted in sub-
  stantially the manner and at the time required herein.
     Article VIII, Section 135 of the Charter of the City of San
  Bernardino is amended to read as follows:
     Section 135. Demands against the City, except those re-
  lating to bonds, or payable from funds not controlled by the
  Mayor and Common Council, or those otherwise exempted by
  law, for which appropriations have been made or authorization
  given in accordance with the Charter, before being paid, shall
  be presented for approval to the Director of Finance or other
  authorized officer, who shall present a register of approved de-
  mands to the Mayor and Common Council for approval prior
  to their payment. Demands for which no appropriations have
  been made or authorization given shall be presented by the
  City Administrator, or other authorized officer, with his recom-
  mendations to the Mayor and Common Council for approval or
  disapproval.
     Any person dissatisfied with the refusal to approve any de-
  mand, in whole or in part, may present the same to the Mayor
, and Common Council which after examining into the matter
  may approve or disapprove the demand in whole or in part.
  The Director of Finance or other authorized officer shall pre-
  pare warrants for all such approved demands, which shall be
  signed by the Mayor and countersigned by the City Clerk.
     Every demand against the City Treasury which may have
  been incurred or authorized by the Board of Water Commis-
  sioners or the Board of Trustees of the Free Public Library
  shall be presented to the board incurring or authorizing the
  indebtedness, which shall approve or disapprove the same. A t
  least a majority vote of all the members of any board or com-
  mission shall be necessary to approve any demand. Each de-
  mand when so approved shall be paid by a warrant on the City
  Treasury payable out of the proper fund and signed by the
  president and secretary of the board which shall have ap-
  proved the same.

  ceedings. He shall have full power and authority to take all
  affidavits and administer all oaths necessary in the transaction
  of city business, but shall make no charge therefor. His official

                EESOLUTION CHAPTEE 50

Assembly   Joint Resolution No. 8—Relative            to the Pure      Air
                          Act of 1968.
           [Filed -with Secretary of State February 28, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, Seventy percent of the poisonous smog which each
year costs California approximately half a billion dollars is
caused by motor vehicles; and
   WHEREAS, The California State Legislature last year devel-
oped vehicle emission standards which all new vehicles must
meet beginning in 1970 and which become increasingly more
stringent through 1974; and
   WHEREAS, California may not implement these standards
unless the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare finds,
under the Federal Air Quality Act of 1967, that the standards
are technically feasible and capable of implementation with
reasonable economic cost; and
   WHEREAS, The standards in the Pure Air Act of 1968 have
been found to be technically feasible and capable of implemen-
tation with reasonable economic cost by a technical advisory
panel of nine California engineers, scientists, and air pollution
experts; and
   WHEREAS, The automobile manufacturers have repeatedly
asked that emission standards be established well in advance
so that they may have "lead t i m e " to develop the hardware
to implement the standards; and
   WHEREAS, All the standards in the Pure Air Act of 1968
are now California state law: the standards for cars as well
as larger vehicles, the standards for exhaust emissions as well
as evaporative loss, and the standards for 1971, 1972, 1973,
and 1974 as well as 1970; and
   WHEREAS, This is the law passed by both houses of the Legis-
lature, and this is the law signed by the Governor; and
 „ WHEREAS, On November 20, 1968, the California Air He-
sources Board unanimously adopted test procedures for all
the standards in the Pure Air Act: for both exhaust and evap-
orative loss; for hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide and oxides of
nitrogen; and for 1970, 1971, 1972, 1973, and 1974; and
   WHEREAS, Without the strong responsible standards in the
Pure Air Act of 1968 there is persuasive medical evidence that
California faces a public health crisis of major dimension;
now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Assembly and Senate of the State of Cali-
fornia, jointly, That the Legislature of the State of California
requests the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare to
grant California a waiver on all of the standards and pro-
cedures in the Pure Air Act of 1968 as promptly as possible;
and be it further
                        1969
Ees. Ch. 52]                   REGULAR SESSION                  3 6 09

  Resolved, That the Chief Clerk of the Assembly transmit
copies of this resolution to the Secretary of Health, Education,
and "Welfare and to each Senator and Representative from
California in the Congress of the United States.

               EESOLUTION CHAPTEE 53
Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 44—Relative to the Senate
                      and Assembly.
            [Filed with Secretary of State March 5, 1969.]

   Resolved by the Senate of the State of California, the As-
sembly thereof concurring, as follows:
   First, That each house of the Legislature shall be in recess
from adjournment of its session on Friday, March 28th, until
the time set for reconvening on Monday, April 7th.
   Second, That no bill shall be introduced after April 8th at
this session except as follows:
   (a) A written notice of intention to introduce a bill, a copy
of the bill, and a digest shall be filed with the Chief Clerk of
the Assembly or the Secretary of the Senate, as the case may
be, and shall be transmitted to the Eules Committee of the
appropriate house. The notice and digest shall be printed in
the journal of that house.
   (b) The Rules Committee of the Assembly or Senate, as the
case may be, shall determine whether there exists an urgent
need for the introduction of the proposed bill.
   (c) If the Eules Committee recommends that introduction
of the proposed bill be permitted, the member may offer a
resolution, without further reference thereof to committee,
granting permission to introduce the bill. The adoption of the
resolution granting such permission shall require an affirma-
tive recorded vote of two-thirds of the elected members of the
house in which the request is made.
   As used in the provision " b i l l " includes constitutional
amendments but does not include joint or concurrent resolu-
tions.
   Third, That all requests for the preparation of a bill to be
introduced on or before April 8th shall be made to the Legis-
lative Counsel on or before March 28th. The Legislative Coun-
sel shall not deliver the draft of any bill requested after
March 28th until April 9th or after.

             [Filed with Secretary of State March 6, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, The 1965 Legislature recognized the need for a
thorough and long-range study of California's system of higher
education, and the Joint Committee on Higher Education was
 thereby created by the Legislature through the adoption of
Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 156 (Resolutions Chapter
 216, Statutes of 1965) ; and
   WHEREAS, There is a continuing need for the Legislature to
review the California Master Plan for Higher Education; and
   WHEREAS, There is a need for further study of alternate
proposals for improving the quality and effectiveness of higher
educational institutions in California; and
   WHEREAS, There is a need for a thorough analysis and study
by the Legislature of major issues in the field of higher edu-
cation before adopting a public policy in this sensitive field;
and
   WHEREAS, There is a need to involve the public and the
higher education community in a search for ways and means
to continue California's recognized leadership in this impor-
tant field; now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Assembly of the State of California, the Sen-
ate thereof concurring, As follows:
   1. The Joint Committee on Higher Education is hereby cre-
ated and authorized and directed to ascertain, study and
analyze all facts relating to existing and emerging problems of
higher education in the State of California, including, but not
limited to, the operation, effect, administration, enforcement
and needed revision of any and all laws in any way bearing
upon or relating to the subject of this resolution, and to report
thereon to the Legislature, including in the report its recom-
mendations for appropriate legislation.
   2. The committee shall consist of five Members of the Sen-
ate, appointed by the Committee on Rules thereof, and five
                    1969
Res. Ch. 56]               REGULAR SESSION                   3513

Members of the Assembly, appointed by the Speaker thereof.
Vacancies occurring in the membership of the committee shall
be filled by the appointing power.
   3. The committee is authorized to act during this session of
the Legislature, including any recess, and after final adjourn-
ment until the commencement of the 1970 Regular Session,
with authority to file its final report not later than the fifth
legislative day of that session.
   4. The committee and each subcommittee thereof is author-
ized to leave the State of California in the performance of its
duties.
   5. The committee and its members shall have and exercise
all of the rights, duties and powers conferred upon investi-
gating committees and their members by the provisions of the
Joint Rules of the Senate and Assembly as they are adopted
and amended from time to time at this session, which provi-
sions are incorporated herein and made applicable to this
committee and its members.
   6. The committee has the following additional powers and
duties:
   (a) To select a chairman and vice chairman from its mem-
bership.
   (b) To contract with such other agencies, public or private,
as it deems necessary for the rendition and affording of such
services, facilities, studies and reports to the committee as will
best assist it to carry out the purposes for which it is created.
   (c) To cooperate with and secure the cooperation of county,
city, city and county, and other local law enforcement agencies
in investigating any matter within the scope of this resolution
and to direct the sheriff of any county to serve subpoenas,
orders and other process issued by the committee.
   (d) To report its findings and recommendations to the Leg-
islature and to the people from time to time and at any time,
not later than herein provided.
   (e) To do any and all other things necessary or convenient
to enable it fully and adequately to exercise its powers, per-
form its duties, and accomplish the objects and purposes of
this resolution.
   7. The sum of one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) or
so much thereof as may be necessary is hereby made available
from the Contingent Funds of the Assembly and Senate for
the expenses of the committee and its members and for any
charges, expenses or claims it may incur under this resolution,
to be paid from the said fund and disbursed, after certification
by the chairman of the committee, upon warrants drawn by
the State Controller upon the State Treasurer.

               RESOLUTION CHAPTER 63
Assembly Joint Resolution No. 10—Relative to the issuing of
  a commemorative stamp and a presidential      proclamation
  upon the centennial of Japanese immigration to the United
  States of America.
           [Filed with Secretary of State March 12, 1969.]

    WHEREAS, The first group of Japanese immigrants arrived
from Aizu "Wakamatsu, Japan, aboard the sidewheeler
 '' China'' of The Pacific Mail Steamship Company and entered
the United States on May 27, 1869, at San Francisco; and
    "WHEEEAS, This valiant and brave band of colonists pro-
ceeded to Sacramento by riverboat, traveled overland by
wagon to Placerville and Gold Hill, and established the Waka-
matsu Tea and Silk Farm Colony of Gold Hill by clearing the
land, building their homes, and cultivating plants and seeds,
including 50,000 three-year-old mulberry trees for silk farm-
ing, which they had brought with them from their native
land; and
    WHEREAS, Although this pioneer project was doomed in less
than two years by a combination of dry climate and a scarcity
of irrigation water, it nevertheless heralded a period during
which the Japanese people immigrated to California to partici-
pate in the beginnings of the Golden State's agricultural in-
dustry ; and
    WHEREAS, On December 16, 1966, the Historical Landmarks
Advisory Committee of the Division of Beaches and Parks
unanimously approved the Wakamatsu Tea and Silk F a r m
  Colony of Gold Hill as a historical landmark and stated that
  "Although the Wakamatsu Tea and Silk Farm Colony was
  short lived and suffered its tragic ending, it signaled the
3620               STATUTES OF CALIFORNIA                 [Res. Ch. 64

coming of Japanese pioneers to America and the beginning of
their notable contribution to the agricultural industry of Cali-
fornia. During the past three-quarters of the century, they
have left their marks in the teeming valleys throughout the
length and breadth of this great state. Many descendants are
carrying on the work of their pioneer forebears with the
same devotion, determination and skill which helped to make
California the most productive farming state in the United
States and the greatest agricultural region in the world . . . " ;
and
   WHEREAS, On June 7, 1969, a monument bearing the state
historical plaque will be dedicated in appropriate ceremonies
at Gold Hill, and the ceremonies will be attended by persons
from many parts of our nation who are of Japanese descent as
well as visitors from J a p a n ; now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Assembly and Senate of the State of Cali-
fornia, jointly, That the Legislature of the State of California
recommend that the Post Office Department of the United
States of America print a commemorative stamp honoring the
centennial of Japanese immigration to the United States of

                RESOLUTION CHAPTER 65
Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 56—Relative to commending
          Frank Burrill and R. L. "Cuba" Morris.
            TFiled with Secretary of State March 13, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, Driver education and driver training are now
recognized as a most important and essential segment of the
total traffic safety program in the State of California; and
   WHEREAS, The people of the state, educators, legislators,
highway safety and law enforcement agencies, and many others
endorse, support and encourage the high school level teaching
of driver education and training as an integral part of the
education of our youth; and
   WHEREAS, The development of this educational pursuit of
increased traffic safety for the young people of our society has
been accomplished through extensive research and development
through the years, but began as the dream and inspiration of
two men, Frank Burrill and R. L. " Cuba'' Morris; and
   WHEREAS, Because of their foresight, unselfish diligence and
dedication Prank Burrill and R. L. " C u b a " Morris gave much
in the way of time, thought, energy, money, and personal
sacrifice to draft and urge the passage of the first legislation
to create programs for driver training as part of high school
curriculum; and
   WHEREAS, Frank Burrill and R. L. " Cuba'' Morris, together
with then Assemblyman Earl W. Stanley of Orange County,
drafted the bill which came to be known as the "Stanley Bill
for Driver Education," and with the help of then Speaker of
the House Sam Collins, organized grass roots support, sold the
idea to schools, parent groups, city and county government
bodies, civic clubs, insurance companies, automobile clubs, auto
manufacturers, and legislators, and, as a result of such
dedicated effort, the bill passed both houses June 20, 1947; and
   WHEREAS, After the passage of the ' ' Stanley Bill for Driver
Education," Frank Burrill and Cuba Morris continued to
develop public support for this vital program by giving talks,
visiting school board members, administrators and teachers;
and
   WHEREAS, Mr. Burrill wrote to all the automobile manufac-
turers and asked them to offer cars for high school use in the
programs, and by persistence and persuasive argument over-
came the companies' initial reluctance and soon the program
of loaning cars to schools became a reality through the coopera-
tive efforts of auto clubs and auto dealers' associations; and
                         1969 R
Res. Ch. 66]                      EGTJLAK SESSION                 3623

   WHEREAS, Mr. Morris and Mr. Burrill established several
course outlines for some of the first driver education classes
which have been used throughout the state; and
   WHEREAS, Mr. Burrill and Mr. Morris developed night school
driver education training for adults and others who had missed
such training in high school and worked with judges to get
violators to attend driver education classes in place of fines;
and
   WHEREAS, In view of the lives which have been saved by the
better driving habits of graduates of driver education and
training classes, and the mature responsibility for the safety
of others which is learned as part of these courses,- now, there-
fore, be it
  Resolved by the Senate of the State of California, the As-
sembly thereof concurring, That the members commend Frank
Burrill and R. L. " C u b a " Morris for their vital part in the
passage of the law creating driver education and training as a
part of high school curriculum; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit suitably
prepared copies of this resolution to Frank Burrill and R. L.
"Cuba "Morris.

             [Piled with Secretary of State March 19, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, The Members of the Assembly were saddened
to learn of the death of Mr. Y. Frank Freeman, former vice
president in charge of Paramount Studio operations; and
   WHEREAS, Y. Frank Freeman was born December 14, 1890,
in Greenville, Georgia, and graduated from Georgia Tech
with an electrical engineering degree in 1910; and
   WHEREAS, He entered the telephone business in Ocilla,
Georgia, which was his first direct contact with the public as
a supplier of goods and services, and later directed his
father's cotton operations; and
    WHEREAS, Mr. Freeman began his career in the motion pic-
ture industry by operating the Amusu Theatre in Fitzgerald,
Georgia, for his father-in-law, developing an interest in both
chain exhibition and distribution; and
    WHEREAS, After joining Lynch Enterprises, which dis-
tributed Paramount and Triangle pictures, he became general
sales manager in 1916 and later became vice president and
general manager of Southern Enterprises in 1919, which dis-
tributed films to 11 southern states; and
    WHEREAS, Y. Frank Freeman supervised the enormous real
estate holdings of Paramount and in 1934 assumed the direc-
 tion of theater operations, and in 1936 was elected vice presi-
 dent in charge of theater operations, which extended his re-
                   1969
Ees. Ch. 71]              REGULAR SESSION                 3629

sponsibility to over 1,400 United States and Canadian theaters
of the Paramount circuit, the largest in the world, and was
also made a board member of Paramount because of the out-
standing leadership he had demonstrated in guiding the
affairs of the company; and
   WHEREAS, He became vice president in charge of the Para-
mount Studios in Hollywood in 1938 and directed its opera-
tions until 1959; and
   WHEREAS, He was recognized as an outstanding motion pic-
ture executive by the film industry, having been elected a
three-term president and board chairman of the Association
of Motion Picture and Television Producers, governor of the
Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, and chair-
man of the Motion Picture Eesearch Council; and
   WHEREAS, He was deeply involved in humanitarian activi-
ties, including three-term campaign chairman and past

eration and Community Chest and as a result of his activities
was the first recipient of the Jean Hersholt Award for Hu-
manitarianism awarded by the Academy of Motion Picture
Arts and Sciences in 1957; and
   WHEREAS, He was active in banking and civic affairs, hav-

                    RESOLUTION CHAPTER 75
Assembly Joint Resolution No. 12—Relative to flood control
              and water reclamation assistance.
                [Filed with Secretary of State March 25, 1969.]

  WHEREAS, Many areas in California were devastated by floods
during the period January 22 through 27, 1969, causing loss
of life and destruction to public and private property; and
3632               STATUTES OP CALIFORNIA                  [Res. Ch. 76

   WHEREAS, The Governor of California has declared 27 coun-
ties in the state as disaster areas so victims of the flood may be
assisted in the repair of their properties and obtain necessary
relief; and
   WHEREAS, Eecent reports showed that existing flood control
projects, financed in part by the federal government were in-
strumental in preventing more damage than had been inflicted;
and
   WHEREAS, California is in the midst of a major flood con-
trol development program and has requested financial assist-
ance in the sum of $190,589,000 from the federal government
for flood control and water reclamation programs for the fiscal
year, 1969-1970; and
   WHEREAS, The President's budget for 1969-1970 includes
only $95,029,000 of the amount requested for flood control and
 water reclamation; and
   WHEREAS, The California Water Commission and the State
Department of Water Eesources has expressed great concern
 over those projects which were not funded, because it would
 delay some of the needed projects; now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Assembly and Senate of the State of Cali-
fornia, jointly, That the Legislature of the State of California
 respectfully memorializes the President and the Congress of
 the United States to review the proposed flood control and
 water reclamation budget for California for the purpose of
 including within the federal budget those projects which were
 recommended but deleted so that the development of those
 projects can be expedited as a means of preventing the loss
 of further life and destruction of property in California; and
 be it further
   Resolved, That the Chief Clerk of the Assembly transmit
 copies of this resolution to the President and Vice President
 of the United States, to the Speaker of the House of Repre-
 sentatives, and to each Senator and Representative from Cali-
 fornia in the Congress of the United States.

               RESOLUTION CHAPTER 78
       Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 69—Relative to
              Spanish-American Veterans Month.
           [Filed with Secretary of State March 25, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, The year 1898 ushered in the age of modern
warfare first fought on a global scale, the same year saw the
emergence of the United States as a world power, and the
United States was engaged in conflict with Spain from April
21 to August 8,1898; and
   WHEREAS, Seventy-one years have passed since this country
fought the battles of the Spanish-American War in which
over 300,000 American armed forces members participated in
answer to President William McKinley's call to arms; and
   WHEREAS, Less than 8,000 of these gallant men and women
still survive to answer the muster of Spanish-American War
veterans, and less than 1,000 of these courageous fighting men
and brave nurses reside in the State of California; and
   WHEREAS, Thirty of these distinguished heroes of the Span-
ish-American War now reside at the Veterans Home of Cali-
fornia, Yountville, which opened its doors to accept its first
members on April 1, 1884, and has now been established as
California Registered Historical Landmark No. 828; now,
therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Senate of the State of California, the As-
sembly thereof concurring, That the Legislature hereby urges
the Governor of the State of California to proclaim the month
of April 1969 as Spanish-American Veterans Month and
hereby urges that all citizens of California prepare suitable
                        1969
Res. Ch. 801                   REGULAR SESSION                   3635
ceremonies honoring the living and the dead of the Spanish-
American W a r ; and be it further
  Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit a copy
of this resolution to the Governor of the State of California.

                     RESOLUTION CHAPTER 92
Assembly Joint Resolution No. 7—Relating to federal indem-
      nity for tuberculosis or brucellosis reacting cattle.
                 [Filed with Secretary of State April 11, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, A S originally conceived, the loss incurred for
cattle slaughtered because they were found to be tuberculosis
or brucellosis reactors was to be equally apportioned one-third
to the state, one-third to the federal government, and one-third
to the owner of the animal; and
   WHEREAS, This formula is only just and equitable in view
of the benefit to the state and nation from this program of
disease control; and
   WHEREAS, Both the federal and state implementing statutes
and regulations provide for a maximum amount to be paid for
each such grade animal or purebred animal; and
   WHEREAS, The California maximum is $50 for a grade ani-
mal and $75 for a purebred animal for tuberculosis reactors,
 and is $75 for a grade animal and $100 for a purebred animal
for brucellosis reactors, but the federal maximum is only $25
for a grade animal and $50 for a purebred animal for both
 diseases; and
   WHEREAS, I t is proposed that the maximum share for the
 State of California be raised to $100 for any grade animal and
 $125 for any purebred animal for both diseases; and
   WHEREAS, The unrealistic federal maximum results in the
 owner of the animal being required to bear a substantially dis-
 proportionate share of the loss, as illustrated by a recent survey
 in California; and
   WHEREAS, The only fair and just share of the federal govern-
 ment would be the contemplated one-third share; now, there-
 fore, be it

   WHEREAS, There has been a steady migration of Mexican

   WHEREAS, Cultural awareness includes informing all Cali-
fornians of the contributions of Mexican-Americans to our
heritage and of California's role in improving and enhanc-
ing the betterment of this group from early childhood through
higher education; and
   WHEREAS, Unlimited possibilities in California's future,
through broadened and expanded educational opportunities,
are being opened to Californians of Mexican descent, who
should be encouraged to take advantage of these opportunities;
now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Assembly of the State of California, the

                 RESOLUTION CHAPTER 98
         Assembly Joint Resolution No. 11—Relative to
                 offshore oil and gas operations.
             [Filed with Secretary of State April 14, 1969.]

    WHEREAS, The great scenic beauty of the California coast-
 line and the coastal fish and wildlife resources of the state are
 threatened with imminent damage and destruction from a mas-
 sive flow of crude petroleum from an oil leak at an oil and gas
 operation off the Santa Barbara coast; and
    WHEEEAS, Such operations are under federal regulation and
 the State of California has had no voice in the granting of
 offshore oil and gas leases by the federal government, although
 the terrible danger these operations represent to the coastal
 resources of the state is now tragically evident; now, there-
 fore, be it
    Resolved by the Assembly and Senate of the State of Cali-
 fornia, jointly, That the Legislature of the State of California
respectfully memorializes the President and the Congress of
 the United States to obtain the approval of the State of Cali-
fornia with respect to any future oil and gas exploration or
development operations off the California coast prior to the
permitting of such operations on federal lands; and be it
further
   Resolved, That the Chief Clerk of the Assembly transmit
copies of this resolution to the President and Vice President of
the United States, to the Speaker of the House of Representa-
tives, to the Secretary of the Interior, and to each Senator
and Representative from California in the Congress of the
United States.

   WHEREAS, The site of the City of Palo Alto was discovered

quito Creek under a centuries-old redwood tree, naming it El
Palo Alto, meaning " t h e tall stick"; and
   WHEREAS, The city was founded in 1889 as University Park
and later renamed in 1892 as Palo Alto after the Palo Alto
Farm established by Senator Leland Stanford, which later
became the site of Stanford University; and
   WHEREAS, In January 1893, when the Palo Alto Times was
first published, the population of Palo Alto reached 400; the
city was incorporated on April 16, 1894, and in 1925, follow-
ing a heated annexation campaign, Mayfield became a part
of the city, increasing the population of 9,000 by 1,700, thus
insuring the continued growth of Palo Alto as a fine com-
munity of superior residential qualities for its present 58,000
residents; and
                      1969
Res. Ch. 106]                REGULAR SESSION                  3655
    "WHEREAS, I t is the home of the world-renowned Stanford
 University, ranked as one of the top 10 universities in the na-
 tion, founded "where the rolling foothills r i s e " in 1891 by
 Senator Stanford, who declared, after the untimely death of
his 16-year old son, Leland Stanford, Jr., in 1884, that " t h e
children of California shall be my children''; and
    WHEREAS, Largely through the pioneering work in elec-
tronics by the Varian Brothers and Hewlett-Packard, Palo
Alto has become one of the two electronic industry centers in
the nation; and
    WHEREAS, With two veterans' hospitals, the Palo Alto Medi-
cal Research Foundation, the Palo Alto Clinic, and the School
of Medicine, Medical Center, and Hospital Center of Stanford
University, the city has become a center of medical research,
as exemplified by the first implantation of the human heart
in this country; now, therefore, be it

   Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit a copy
of this resolution to the Governor and a suitably prepared
copy of this resolution to the Honorable Frances K. Dias,
Mayor of Palo Alto.

   That at the Special Municipal Election, Charter Amend-

   That Charter Amendment No. 1 so ratified by the electors
of the City of Glendale is in words and figures as follows:

                   Charter Amendment No. 1
    Section 11 of Article V I of the Charter of the City of Glen-
 dale is amended to read:
   "(Article VI) Section 11. Official Advertising. All offi-
 cial advertising of the city shall be done in one or more news-
papers of general circulation, as defined by the laws of the
 State of California, which shall be published in the City of
 Glendale. The council shall annually call for bids for such
advertising pursuant to specifications which shall first be ap-
proved by the council, and shall award any and all such con-
tracts to the lowest responsible bidder; provided, that the
council may reject all bids and may again call for bids; and
provided further, that no defect or irregularity in proceedings
taken under this section shall invalidate any publication when
the same is otherwise in conformity to law or this Charter."
   That at the Special Municipal Election, Charter Amend-
ment No. 2 was ratified by a majority of the electors of the
City voting thereon.
   That Charter Amendment No. 2 so ratified by the electors
of the City of Glendale is in words and figures as follows:

                  Charter Amendment No. 2
   Section 6 of Article VI of the Charter of the City of Glen-
dale is amended to read:
  "(Article VI) Section 6. Ordinances generally. The en-
acting clause of every ordinance passed by the council shall
be: 'Be it ordained by the Council of the City of Glendale.'
The enacting clause of every ordinance initiated by the people
shall b e : 'Be it ordained by the people of the City of Glen-
dale.' At least five days must elapse between the introduction
and the final passage of any ordinance; provided, that amend-
ment germane to the subject of any proposed ordinance may
be made when it is brought up for final passage; and provided
further, that in case of an extraordinary epedemic or any dis-
aster, such as flood, fire or earthquake, requiring immediate
3660              STATUTES OF CALIFORNIA            [ReS. Ch. 108

action on the part of any public authorities, an emergency
ordinance may be introduced and passed at either a regular
or special meeting without any intervention of time between
introduction and final passage. A final vote on any ordinance
or any vote on any appropriation must be taken only at a reg-
ular or adjourned regular meeting. Every ordinance must be
signed by the mayor and attested by the clerk. Notice thereof
shall be published once in a newspaper of general circulation.
Any ordinance granting any franchise or privilege shall be
published at the expense of the applicant therefor.
   In the publication of every ordinance the advertisement
shall contain a statement of the title, number and date of the
ordinance, a brief statement of the nature of the ordinance,
and a reference to a copy of the ordinance which shall be on
file and available for public inspection at all reasonable times
in the office of the city clerk.''

                KESOLUTION CHAPTER 112
Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 94—Relative to commend-
  ing the California Farm Bureau Federation on its golden
  anniversary.
            [Filed with Secretary of State April 17, 1969.3

   WHEREAS, The California F a r m Bureau Federation is com-
memorating its golden anniversary as the organizational tool
through which the farmers have worked to improve their farm-
ing methods and conditions, to reduce their costs, and to im-
prove their marketing capability; and
   WHEREAS, The Farm Bureau was organized in November
1919, to coordinate the efforts of 32 county farm bureaus with
a then combined membership of 24,168 which had been formed
to be the channels through which county farm advisers and
extension specialists of the University of California would
work in bringing to the individual farm operator and his fam-
ily the latest in agricultural research; and
   WHEREAS, The Farm Bureau did not merely confine itself
to educational activities, but helped to form many marketing
cooperatives and organizations to aid the farmer to obtain a
fair market price for his products and was instrumental in
obtaining the enactment of the California Marketing Act in
1937 under which the State Marketing Orders are operated;
and
   WHEREAS, Its enlightened attitude led to the develop-
ment of many programs, which were subsequently enacted,
aimed at the eradication of disease, establishing sanitary con-
ditions for the production of milk, setting up of meat inspec-
3664                 STATUTES OF CALIFORNIA                 [Res. Ch. 113

tion practices, and setting quality standards for many com-
modities ; and
   WHEREAS, Largely through its efforts, water studies were
continued in the 1920's and finally became the Statewide
Water Plan in 1930 and the enactment of the Central Valley
Project Act of 1933 which authorized the construction of the
CVP, and in 1958 it formed the Inter-Organization Water
Committee to solidify support for the Burns-Porter Bond Act
which was approved by the voters in 1960 to finance the con-
struction of the State Water Project; and
   WHEREAS, TO preserve the prime agricultural land of this
state, the Farm Bureau led the battle to obtain the enactment
of the California Land Conservation Act of 1965, which pro-
vides for assessing agricultural land on the basis of other than
market value, and the adoption of the Open Space Amend-
ment authorizing the Legislature to define open space and de-
vise a method of assessing such lands on the basis of other
than full cash value; and
   WHEREAS, Realizing that the future of agriculture lies in
the hands of our youth, the Farm Bureau in 1967 reorga-
nized the Young People's Department, which was created in
1947, into a Committee of California Young Farmers and
Ranchers and in 1953 established the California Farm Bureau
Scholarship Foundation, which has granted five scholarships
annually since 1954; and
   WHEREAS, Cognizance of the importance of agriculture to
the developing nations of the world, the Farm Bureau formed
the Cal-Farm Travel Service in 1955 to arrange "farmer-to-
farmer" tours throughout the world and has sponsored sev-
eral trainee programs for young farmers, including the Young
Visiting Japanese Farmers Trainee Program, from Europe,
Latin America, Asia, and the Near East; now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Assembly of the State of California, the
Senate thereof concurring, That the members commend the
California Farm Bureau Federation on its golden anniversary
for distinguished service, symbolizing "Progress in the Past—•
Promise for the F u t u r e , ' ' rendered to the farmers, to the state,
and to the nation; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Chief Clerk of the Assembly transmit
a suitably prepared copy of this resolution to the California
Farm Bureau Federation.

               RESOLUTION CHAPTER 116
        Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 68—Relative to
                       Law Day, U.S.A.
             [Filed with Secretary of State April 21, 1969.]

  WHEREAS, I t has come to the attention of the Members of the
Senate and the Assembly that the theme for Law Day, U.S.A.,
                      1969
Res. Ch. 117]                REGULAR SESSION                  3667
 to be observed on May 1, 1969, will be Justice and Equality
 Depend Upon Law and You; and
    WHEREAS, Every good citizen recognizes that representative
 government depends for its vitality and strength upon citizen
 participation in its processes and the broader the participation
 the more effective and just the government will be; and
    WHEREAS, Every citizen has a responsibility to his country,
 state, and local community to observe the laws, to support the
 law enforcement agencies and the courts, to recognize the
 rights of others, and to assist in advancing the equality of
 justice and opportunity for all Americans; and
    WHEREAS, Our form of government, which has protected our
nation for over 190 years, requires that the right of dissent
 and the right to petition for redress of grievances be asserted
 in a lawful manner, since in a free society the end to be
sought, however worthy, can never justify unlawful means;
and
   WHEREAS, It is appropriate that on this special day, which
was set aside by joint resolution of Congress and by presiden-
tial proclamation, we should reaffirm our faith in the will of
law and in the supremacy of government by law rather than
by men; and
   WHEREAS, The members commend the organized bar for its
vigorous programs and educational activities which emphasize
the importance of law in our society and for its efforts in
promoting the observance of Law Day throughout the nation;
now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Senate of the State of California, the Assem-
bly thereof concurring, That the Governor of the State of Cali-
fornia is respectfully requested to proclaim Thursday, May 1,
1969, as Law Day, U.S.A., throughout this state, and to call
upon all the citizens to join in its observance through appro-
priate ceremonies, programs and educational activities, and
through a rededication to the ideals of equality and justice for
all; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit a copy
of this resolution to the Honorable Ronald Reagan, Governor
of the State of California, and suitably prepared copies to
William T. Gossett, President of the American Bar Associa-
tion, and Samuel 0 . Pruitt, Jr., President of the State Bar of
California.

                RESOLUTION CHAPTER 117
      Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 84—Relative
           to the retirement of William A. Kerlin.
            [Filed with Secretary of State April 22, 1969.]

  WHEREAS, William A. Kerlin, Chief of the California De-
partment of Agriculture's Bureau of Weights and Measures
3668               STATUTES OF CALIFORNIA                 [EeS. Ch. 118

since 1960, will retire on May 1st after more than 37 years
of dedicated service to the people of the State of California;
and
   WHEREAS, A pioneer in the use of statistical sampling tech-
niques in state inspection and enforcement activities, Mr. Ker-
lin has administered a bureau responsible for enforcing Cali-
fornia weights and measures laws, including the supervision
of the 58 county sealers of weights and measures; and
   WHEREAS, In 1960 Mr. Kerlin played the key role in writ-
ing the California statute which first established a statisti-
cally valid sampling technique to be used in enforcing weights
and measures laws, which has since served as a model for
many other agencies around the country; and
   WHEREAS, A native of Hastings, Nebraska, Mr. Kerlin came
to California in 1916 and after attending San Jose State Col-
lege, he became a surveyor in the Santa Clara County Engi-
neer's office and then deputy county sealer, a post he held for
nine years; and
   WHEREAS, After qualifying by competitive examination, he
was appointed Alameda County Sealer of Weights and Meas-
ures and 14 years later, he joined the California Department
of Agriculture as Chief of the Bureau of Weights and Meas-
ures ; and
   WHEREAS, Mr. Kerlin is presently chairman of the Laws
and Regulations Committee, National Conference on Weights
and Measures; a member of the Special Weights and Measures
Committee of the Federal Trade Commission; and a member
of the Special Weights and Measures Committee of the Fed-
eral Food and Drug Administration; now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Assembly of the State of California, the
Senate thereof concurring, That the members commend Wil-
liam A. Kerlin for his many years of dedicated public serv-
ice and wish him happiness and success in his future endeav-
ors ; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Chief Clerk of the Assembly transmit
a suitably prepared copy of this resolution to William A.
Kerlin.

   That the City of Pomona now is and at all times herein

the Council of said city did, on its own motion, cause to be

city; that at a regular meeting held February 10, 1969, said

election to be held in said city for the purpose of submitting to

The Progress Bulletin, the official newspaper of said city and
a newspaper of general circulation printed and published in
said city, on February 14, 1969, and in each edition thereof
during the day of publication; that said date of publication was
within 15 days after said proposed charter amendment was
filed with the City Clerk and said election was held not less
than 40 nor more than 60 days after the completion of said
advertising in said official newspaper;

posed charter amendment and continuing until the day fixed
for said election, a notice was published and advertised in said

 amendment may be had upon application therefor at the office
 of the City Clerk of said city; that such copies were so avail-
 able ; that copies of said proposed charter were printed in con-
 venient pamphlet form and in type of not less than 10-point
 and copies thereof were mailed to each of the qualified electors

3670               STATUTES OF CALIFORNIA            [Res. Ch. 118

charter of said city and by law on April 8, 1969; that the fol-
lowing said election returns of said election were duly can-
vassed as provided by law and the results of said canvass were
certified to said Council and said Council thereupon, by resolu-
tion, entered into its minutes, declared the results of the
canvass of the returns of said election, and found, determined
and declared that a majority of the qualified voters voting
upon said proposed charter amendment at said election voted
in favor of such proposed charter amendment and that said
charter amendment shall be deemed ratified and shall be sub-
mitted to the Legislature at its present session; that the re-
sults as so declared show that at said election 6,526 votes were

                  RESOLUTION CHAPTER 120
       Senate Joint Resolution No. 8—Relative to school
                    district appropriations.
                [Piled with Secretary of State April 24, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, The Congress of the United States of America
has appropriated $505.9 million for the fiscal year ending
June 30, 1969, for payments to school districts under the
provisions of Public Law 81-874, estimated to be sufficient
to meet 90 percent of the requirements under the law; and
   WHEREAS, Federal administrative decisions have determined
that only 35 percent of the requirement will be released dur-
ing the fiscal year ending June 30, 1969, to eligible school
districts; and
   WHEREAS, This administrative decision affects adversely
some 438 California school districts, in which in excess of
400,000 eligible pupils reside; and
   WHEREAS, The withholding of these funds will adversely
affect the educational program for more than three million
3672               STATUTES OF CALIFORNIA                  i JJgg QJj# J 2 1

children who attend school in these districts eligible for
funds under Public Law 81-874; and
   WHEREAS, The administrative decisions made will result
in reduction in school support from Public Law 81-874 in
excess of $50 million during the fiscal year; and
   WHEREAS, Under the provisions of Public Law 81-874, the
federal government since 1951 has participated as a local
property taxpayer in school districts impacted with students
of parents employed on federal property which is not sub-
ject to local property taxation; and
   WHEREAS, Such federal participation under full provisions
of the law does not meet the added costs of education caused
by federal activities; and
   WHEREAS, The withholding of these funds by administra-
tive decision is not in accordance with the intent of the
Congress as expressed in Public Law 81-874 and in Section
406 of Title III of Public Law 90-576; and
   WHEREAS, The withholding of these funds will have an
irreparable adverse effect on the majority of school children
in California; now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Senate and Assembly of the State of Cali-
fornia, jointly, That the Legislature of the State of Cali-
fornia respectfully memorializes the President of the United
States, the Director of the Bureau of the Budget and the
 Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare and other in-
volved federal officials to review the existing administrative
decision and to provide for release to eligible school districts
during the 1969 fiscal year the full appropriation authorized
by Congress for that year; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit copies
of this resolution to the President of the United States, the
 Director of the Bureau of the Budget, the Secretary of
Health, Education and Welfare, and to each member of the
California Delegation in Congress.

               RESOLUTION CHAPTER 123
       Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 75—Relative to
          "Livermore Centennial Celebration Day."
            [Filed with Secretary of State April 25, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, I t has come to the attention of the Members that
the City of Livermore will, on October 11, 1969, observe
"Livermore Centennial Celebration D a y " ; and
   WHEREAS, One hundred years ago the first subdivision of
land took place in the Livermore community; and
   WHEREAS, The Livermore Valley was first explored and de-
scribed in 1772 by a party of Spaniards, although it was not
until Mission San Jose was established in 1797 that the valley
began to be used for agriculture, when it was a grazing ground
for the mission cattle and was known as the Valle de San
Jose, with its only inhabitants the native Indian tribes; and
   WHEREAS, The valley was the natural route for Indians, or
anyone else, who wanted to travel toward the coast from
California's central valley and, consequently, it was used by
Indians going to the mission along the coast and by the
soldiers who set out to find and punish the Indians; and
   WHEREAS, With the discovery of gold in California, the
traffic increased in the 1850's, new routes through the valley
were developed, there were surveys for railroads, and in gen-
eral much activity; and
                         1969
Ees. Ch. 124]                   REGULAR SESSION                   3675
   WHEREAS, A settlement named Laddsville developed on the
route chosen for the first railroad through the valley, but by
 the time the first train went through, in 1869, William Men-
 denhall had laid out a new town and named it for the pioneer
Robert Livermore; and
   WHEREAS, The economy of the Livermore Valley was pas-
toral and agricultural; cattle, sheep and horses have always
been important products, as well as hay and grain, and later
on, grapes and wine, truck crops, and roses; animal products,
agricultural products, and a variety of mineral products from
the mines in the hills south of town furnished cargo for the
 railroads, and flour mills and warehouses, to store hay, grain,
 and other products from the ranches, were prominent early
businesses; and
   WHEREAS, A S with most towns, gradual changes in economy
and progress have taken place over the years, some significant
events which influenced the changing pattern being: the de-
velopment of gravel industry, the extension through the valley
by the San Francisco Water Department of the Hetch Hetchy
water and powerlines, the military installations during
World War II, and the State Water Project, with the recent
construction of the South Bay Aqueduct and the Del Valle
Dam; and
   WHEREAS, In the last decade and a half, the establishment
of several atomic energy installations in the area has brought
about a radical change in the economy, culture, population,
and entire character of Livermore and the surrounding area,
which change has been accompanied by a burgeoning popula-
tion which has turned Livermore from a small rural town,
agricultural in nature, to a small city with an industrial out-
look, with the prospect of more rapid growth and change in
the future; now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Senate of the State of California, the As-
sembly thereof concurring, That the members express their
heartiest congratulations to the City of Livermore upon its
centennial celebration and request the Governor to proclaim
October 11,1969, as "Livermore Centennial Celebration D a y " ;
and be it further
   Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit a copy
of this resolution to the Goyernor and a suitably prepared
copy to the City of Livermore.

   WHEREAS, Goodwill Industries had its beginning in 1902,

for donations of repairable household articles and clothing
which could be repaired and sold, thereby providing work and
income for the needy and handicapped; and
   WHEREAS, Vocational rehabilitation of the seriously handi-
capped was the initial goal and Goodwill Industries has since
expanded its activities to encompass the mentally ill and men-
tally retarded in order that these people may live productive
and fulfilling lives; and
   WHEREAS, A S a result of the outstanding efforts of the 11
autonomous Goodwills in the State of California, more than
7,370 handicapped persons have been helped and have re-
ceived $6,493,748 in wages; and
   WHEREAS, Goodwill Industries is a continuing tribute to
the initiative of private groups that provide a source of work
and income for persons who otherwise would be dependent
upon public assistance; and
   WHEREAS, The program of Goodwill Industries, based on the
dignity of man, gives self-respect to the handicapped worker;
now, therefore, be it
  Resolved ~by the Senate of the State of California, the As-
sembly thereof concurring, That the members wish to take this
opportunity to commend the national organization and the
California Goodwill Industries on their outstanding job in
serving the handicapped; and be it further
  Resolved, That the Governor of the State of California is
requested to proclaim the week of May 4 through May 10,
1969, National Goodwill Week, in California; and be it further
  Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit a copy
of this resolution to the Honorable Ronald Reagan, Governor
of the State of California, and suitably prepared copies to
Russell Gwynn, Chairman of the Council of California Good-
wills, and Robert G. Depner, Executive Director of Goodwill
Industries of Central California.

               RESOLUTION CHAPTER 134
Senate Joint Resolution No. 11—Relative to the                Sacramento
               River Bank Protection Project.
             [Filed with Secretary of State May 1, 1969.]

   WHEBEAS, The Sacramento River Bank Protection Project
was authorized by the Flood Control Act of 1960 to provide a
long-range (25 years) program of bank erosion control works
to maintain the integrity of the levee system of the Sacramento
River Flood Control Project so that it can provide the degree
of protection for which it was designed; and
   WHEBEAS, The rains and flooding of the past winter have
caused extensive erosion of riverbank levees; and
                        1969
Res. Ch. 135]                  REGULAR SESSION                 3683

   WHEREAS, The federal appropriations for the Sacramento
River Bank Protection Project, which reached the minimum
required level of 3.5 million dollars during the 1965-1966 fiscal
year, have since dropped to a level of about 1.5 million dollars;
and
   WHEREAS, The present levee funding does not even keep
pace with new erosion, and there is severe danger of a break
in the levee system; and
   WHEREAS, A failure of the levee system could result in
millions of dollars of damages to one of the most productive
agricultural areas in the nation and to the Cities of Sacra-
mento, Marysville, Yuba City, and other communities; and
   WHEREAS, An appropriation of only 2 million dollars is pro-
posed in the budget for the fiscal year 1969-1970, which is
not adequate to keep pace with the present rate of erosion
and will result in a delay of up to two years on all future units
of the project; and
   WHEREAS, The Army Corps of Engineers has indicated that
an annual federal appropriation of $3,500,000 is needed to keep
pace with bank erosion; now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Senate and Assembly of the State of Cali-
fornia, jointly, That the Legislature of the State of California
respectfully memorializes the President and the Congress of
the United States to increase the appropriation for construc-
tion funds for the Sacramento River Bank Protection Project
in the President's Budget for the fiscal year 1969-1970 to a
minimum of 3.5 million dollars; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit copies
of this resolution to the President and Vice President of the
United States, to the Director of the Bureau of the Budget,
to the Chief of Engineers of the Army Corps of Engineers, to
the Speaker of the House of Representatives, and to each Sen-
ator and Representative from California in the Congress of
the United States.

               RESOLUTION CHAPTER 139
Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 121—Relative to the
  anniversary of the Cinco de Mayo as Mexican-American
  Week.
             [Filed with Secretary of State May 1, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, While the United States was engaged in the
tragic Civil War testing the principle upon which this nation
was founded, that " a l l men are created equal . . . that they
are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights,"
its neighbor, the Republic of Mexico, was invaded by an army
of foreign troops from Europe; and
   WHEREAS, This invading foreign army was met at Guada-
lupe Hill near the City of Puebla on the fifth day of May, 1862,
by an outnumbered and untrained Mexican force, under the
command of Ignacio Zaragoza; and
   WHEREAS, The soldiers of Mexico through their great cour-
age and self-sacrifice defeated this invading force in this great
battle; and
   WHEREAS, This victory stands as an encouragement and a
symbol in the long struggle of Mexico against this foreign in-
vader which eventually culminated in the ousting of a mon-
archy, which was established by these foreign troops, and the
reestablishment of Mexico as a sovereign independent nation;
and
   WHEREAS, Cinco de Mayo has since been celebrated the
world over as a day symbolizing the opposition of free peoples
to foreign domination and the triumph of freedom over oppres-
sion ; and
   WHEREAS, This day is recorded in the annals of history along
with the Fourth of July and Bastille Day as one of the great
days in the advancement of human liberty and self-govern-
ment; and
   WHEREAS, Concerned citizens of Mexican ancestry will be
observing the 107th anniversary of this event and will com-
memorate the triumph at Guadalupe Hill, Cinco de Mayo; and
   WHEREAS, Numerous Mexican-American organizations and
the Spanish-speaking community will sponsor appropriate ob-
servances during the week of Cinco de Mayo; and
   WHEREAS, During this week it will be fitting for all Cali-
fornians to contemplate the historical contributions of Mexican
culture and character to the history of this state which en-
riched and advanced our multiracial culture and to acknowl-
edge the contributions of Mexican-American citizens in areas
                       1969
Res. Ch. 140]                 REGULAR SESSION                  3637

of education, labor, industry, government, and the professions;
now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Assembly of the State of California, the Sen-
ate thereof concurring, That the Legislature hereby requests
the Governor to proclaim May 5 through May 11, 1969, as
Mexican-American Week in California and further urges that
the Governor request the California public schools to sponsor
appropriate programs during this week and urge all the people
of this state to take advantage of this opportunity to learn
the role that the Mexican culture has played in the develop-
ment of the United States and the State of California; and be
it further
   Resolved, That the Members of the Legislature of the State
of California extend, on behalf of the people of this state,
their congratulations and felicitous greetings to our Mexican-
American citizens and our neighbors to the south in the
Republic of Mexico on the anniversary of the Battle of Guada-
lupe, Cinco de Mayo, and convey to them our warmest expres-
sion of friendship; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Chief Clerk of the Assembly transmit a
copy of this resolution to the Governor and transmit suitably
prepared copies to Assemblyman Garcia for appropriate dis-
tribution.

Section 404.
   The mayor shall be the presiding officer at all meetings of
the city council and shall have a voice in all its proceedings
but shall not vote except on the appointment or removal of
members of the various boards and commissions and to break
a city council tie-vote which exists for any cause. He shall be
the official head of the city for all ceremonial purposes. He
shall have the primary but not exclusive responsibility for in-
terpreting the policies, programs and needs of the city govern-
ment to the people, and of informing the people of any major
change in policy or program. He shall advise the city council
on all matters of policy and public relations and perform such
other duties as may be prescribed by this Charter.

   The city council shall designate one of its members as mayor
pro tempore, who shall serve in such capacity at the pleasure
of the city council. In addition to his regular duties as council-
man, the mayor pro tempore shall perform the duties of the
mayor during his absence or disability.

Section 419.
  Notwithstanding any other provision of this Charter when
a tie-vote exists for any cause, in order to break that tie, the
mayor shall have the same voting right as a city councilman
for or against the item before the City Council. The mayor's
vote shall be deemed a city councilman's vote for all purposes,
including the introduction or adoption of both ordinances and
resolutions.

by the City of Riverside and its City Council and City Clerk
in the matter of submitting the proposal to amend the City
Charter and in calling, noticing and conducting the election
and certifying the canvass of the returns and declaring the
results thereof.

fixed the seal of the City of Riverside this 15th day of April,

such determination thereafter had been approved or concurred
in by the board; and (b) had certified, in writing, that he had
read and understands the provisions of this section and Sec-

may return the retired member to active duty only in or to a

of any such Beneficiary, (I) if the amount thereof which
shall be payable to such Beneficiary were to be more than the
amount of the pension which had been payable to such mem-
ber, shall include the percentage of any increase in the cost
of living which had been applied to the pension of such mem-
ber, or (II) if the amount thereof which shall be payable to
such Beneficiary were to be less than the amount of the pen-
sion which had been payable to such member, shall include
that portion of the percentage of any increase in the cost of
living which had been applied to the pension of such member
which shall be in the same ratio as the amount of the pension
which shall be payable to such Beneficiary shall bear to the
amount of the pension which had been payable to such mem-
ber, and the percentage of any increase or decrease in the
cost of living in excess of 2% per year which had been carried
over for such member as of the date of his death shall be
carried over for such Beneficiary if (I) hereof were to be
applicable or in the same ratio therein provided if (II) hereof
were to be applicable.
   (3) Whenever the pension of any qualified surviving spouse
hereafter shall be terminated pursuant to any provisions of
Subsection (a) of Section 190.13 and the pension thereafter
shall become payable on behalf of any minor child or children
or dependent child or children of the deceased member, the
amount of pension on behalf of such child or children shall
include that portion of the percentage of increase in the cost
of living which had been applied to the pension of such quali-
fied surviving spouse which shall be in the same ratio as the
amount of the pension which shall be payable on behalf of
such child or children shall bear to the amount of the pension
which had been payable to such qualified surviving spouse, and
the percentage of any increase or decrease in the cost of living
in excess of 2% per year which had been carried over for such
qualified surviving spouse as of the date of the termination of
his or her pension shall be carried over on behalf of such child
or children in the same ratio hereinabove provided.
   (D) The amount of the pension never shall be reduced, by
reason of the application thereto of the provisions of Section
190.14 or this section, to an amount less than the amount
3708              STATUTES OF CALIFORNIA            [Res. Ch. 143

thereof payable pursuant to provisions of this Article other
than those of Section 190.14 and this section.
   (E) Section 190.14 hereafter shall be construed and applied
in accordance with this section as to each pension mentioned
in this section.

                RESOLUTION CHAPTER 144
       Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 147—Relative
                to the death of Paul Claiborne.
                [Piled with Secretary of State May 5, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, I t was with profound sorrow that the members
 learned of the death of Paul Claiborne, a longtime civic leader
 in Placer County and Sacramento County, on April 13, 1969;
 and
   WHEREAS, He was born in Indiana on March 3, 1902, came
to California with his parents, Luther and Rachel Claiborne,
in 1904, attended schools in Placer County while working on
various jobs, including, with his younger brother, Silas, all the
paper routes in Roseville for the Sacramento Bee, Sacramento
Union, San Francisco Chronicle, and San Francisco Examiner;
and
   WHEREAS, After graduating from Heald's Business College
in Sacramento, he served in various capacities with Bradstreet
 Company (later named Dun & Bradstreet), Retailer's Credit
Association of Sacramento, Henning Advertising Service, and
 Equitable Life Assurance Society of New York, and opened
an agency called "Sorenson & Claiborne" in North Sacra-
mento for Star cars; and
   WHEREAS, In 1926, he returned to the Retailer's Credit
Association in Auburn, and promptly became active in nearly
every civic project; and
   WHEREAS, He organized the Placer Savings and Loan Asso-
ciation in 1946 to encourage thrift and help people obtain a
home of their own and served as its president and chairman of
the board until his death; and

               EESOLUTION CIIAPTEE 146
Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 43—Relating to a study of
  tenure in the University of California, the California State
  Colleges, and the public junior colleges.
             [Filed with Secretary of State May 7, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, The laws and administrative regulations govern-
ing the University of California, the California State Colleges,
and the public junior colleges in California establish rules for
the appointment, reappointment, dismissal, and demotion of
academic personnel; and
  WHEREAS, Taken as a whole, those rules establish privileges
of tenure for full-time faculty in regular rank; and
  WHEREAS, There is a wide spectrum of opinion regarding
the value and effect of tenure in the "University of California,
the California State Colleges, and the public junior colleges;
and
                       1969
Res. Ch. 147]                 REGULAR SESSION                  3721
   WHEREAS, Questions are now raised about the objectives and
effects of tenure in the University of California, the California
State Colleges, and the public junior colleges; and
   WHEREAS, Current events in higher education require an
immediate review of this subject so that the laws and adminis-
trative regulations may be kept current with changing circum-
stances; now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Senate of the State of California, the Assem-
bly thereof concurring, That the Legislature hereby directs the
Coordinating Council for Higher Education to study the cur-
rent rules of tenure in the University of California, the Cali-
fornia State Colleges, and the public junior colleges; compare
such rules of tenure in public and private institutions of higher
education in California and in other states; state the objectives
of tenure; and set forth policy alternatives to achieve those
objectives; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Legislature hereby directs the Coordinat-
ing Council for Higher Education to report on the subject of
this resolution as soon as possible but not later than May 8,
1969; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate shall transmit
copies of this resolution to the members of the Coordinating
Council for Higher Education.


                 RESOLUTION C H A P T E R 147
Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 88—Relative to proclaim-
  ing the week of April 27-May 3, 1969, as "Canada-United
  States Goodwill Week."
                [Filed with Secretary of State May 7, 1969.]

   WHEREAS, For more than a century, two of the greatest na-
tions in the world, the United States and Canada, have enjoyed
a close and lasting friendship, and the year 1969 will mark the
102nd aninversary of Canada as a nation and the 152nd an-
niversary of the Rush-Bagot Agreement which demilitarized
the boundary between these two nations; and
   WHEREAS, The Rush-Bagot Agreement established permissi-
ble armament levels for each nation on the Great Lakes, and
was proclaimed by President Monroe on April 28, 1818, to be
effective as of April 28, 1817, the date of an exchange of notes
between Richard Rush, an American lawyer and diplomat who
was Acting Secretary of State for the United States, and Sir
Charles Bagot, a British diplomat and administrator who was
Minister to the United States; and
   WHEREAS, TWO nations, growing greater each decade, have
given a bright example to the nations of a world growing
smaller each decade as measured by communication and trans-
portation by forever distinguishing themselves by neutraliza^
3722               STATUTES OF CALIFORNIA                   [JJ es _ Qh. 148

 tion of the Great Lakes and avoidance of hostile fortification to
the end that today a feeling of high regard, mutual respect,
 and goodwill pervades the relationship between the nations;
 and
     WHEREAS, In 1922, Kiwanis International instituted the ob-
 servance of "Canadian-United States D a y s " to celebrate the
 Eush-Bagot Agreement and the enduring friendship of our
nations, and this observance is now known as ' ' Canada-United
 States Goodwill Week" and is observed each year by Kiwanis
 Clubs throughout the land through efforts to inform people
 on life in our neighboring country, demonstrations of friend-
 liness toward our neighbors themselves, and efforts to improve
 understanding between the two great pioneering nations of
 Kiwanis; and
    WHEREAS, The spirit of friendship existing between the
 United States and Canada was best expressed in the last public
 address of President Warren G. Harding when he said:
       " W h a t an object lesson of peace is shown by our two
    countries to all the world. No grim-faced fortifications mark
    our frontiers, no huge battleships patrol our dividing waters,
    no stealthy spies lurk in our tranquil border hamlets. Only
     a scrap of paper, recording hardly more than a simple un-
     derstanding, safeguards lives and properties on the Great
    Lakes, and only humble mileposts mark the inviolable bound-
    ary line for thousands of miles through farm and forest. Our
    protection is in our fraternity, our armor is our faith, and
    the tie that binds more firmly year after year is ever-increas-
    ing acquaintanceship and comradeship through interchange
    of citizens; and the compact is not of perishable parchment
    but of fair and honorable dealing, which, God grant, shall
    continue for all t i m e ' ' ;
now, therefore, be it
    Resolved by the Senate of the State of California, the Assem-
bly thereof concurring, That the members request the Gov-
ernor to proclaim the week of April 27-May 3, 1969, as
' ' Canada-United States Goodwill Week,'' and urge the citizens
of California to observe the anniversary of the Rush-Bagot
Agreement and the everlasting and historic friendship it has
created between the citizens of our great nation and Canada;
and be it further
    Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit a copy
of this resolution to Governor Reagan and suitably prepared
copies to Kiwanis International and the Kiwanis Club of South
Sacramento.

  Week.

                        1969

   WHEREAS, Transportation is a vital modern-day network
steeped in the history of the "Conestoga" and the " I r o n
Horse" in the days of our westward expansion up to our
present-day supersonic jets, and this transportation system
helps keep the wheels of commerce and industry turning, and
makes us the most mobile society in the history of the world;
and
   WHEREAS, Our personal, commercial, and economic lives, as
well as our national defense, are dependent upon efficient, mod-
ern, and rapid transportation; and
   WHEREAS, The Congress, by Senate Joint Resolution 22 of
May 16, 1957 (71 Stat. 30), has requested the President to
proclaim annually the third Friday of May of each year as
National Defense Transportation Day, and by House Joint
Resolution 628 of May 14, 1962 (76 Stat. 69), has requested
the President to proclaim annually the week of May in which
that Friday falls as National Transportation Week, as a tribute
to the men and women who, working night and day, move the
goods and people throughout our land; and
   WHEREAS, The President has designated Friday, May 16,
1969, as National Defense Transportation Day, and the week
beginning May 11, 1969, as National Transportation Week;
now, therefore, be it
   Resolved by the Senate of the State of California, the As-
sembly thereof concurring, That the members urge all Cali-
f ornians to participate, with representatives of the transporta-
tion industry, our armed services and state and local agencies,
in the observance of these occasions through appropriate cere-
monies ; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Governor is hereby requested to proclaim
the week beginning May 11, 1969, as California Transporta-
tion Week; and be it further
   Resolved, That the Secretary of the Senate transmit a copy
of this resolution to the Governor of the State of California.

         "Section 611. Ordinances and resolutions—
                  Adoption and publication.
   a. No ordinance, other than an emergency ordinance, shall
be adopted by the council within five (5) days after its intro-
duction, nor at other than a regular or an adjourned regular
meeting. At the time of introduction, an ordinance shall be-
come a part of the proceedings of said meeting in the custody
of the city clerk. An ordinance may be introduced by a read-
ing of its title only. Before adoption, it shall be read in full,
unless after reading the title thereof, a further reading is
waived by the unanimous consent of the couneilmen present,
which consent shall be established by a motion and a recorded
roll-call vote.
  b. An ordinance altered or amended after its introduction
and before adoption shall not be adopted within five (5) days
after such alteration or amendment. Such ordinance shall be
reread as altered or amended before adoption unless reread-
ing thereof is waived as provided in subsection (a) hereof.
Corrections of typographical or clerical errors which do not
change the intent expressed in the ordinance shall not be
deemed alterations or amendments within the meaning of this
subsection.
3728               STATUTES OF CALIFORNIA            [KeS. Ch. 151

   c. Every ordinance must be published once in the official
newspaper of the city, or in such other form that it may be
sent to the voters. One copy of every ordinance introduced
shall be posted by the clerk within twenty-four (24) hours
after introductory reading on the public bulletin board in the
Municipal Building of the city.
   d. The clerk shall thereafter note on a posted copy any cor-
rections, alterations or amendments which may occur after the
time of the introductory reading.
   e. Failure of the clerk to post said ordinance or to make
corrections thereon as provided in subsections (c) and (d)
hereof, shall not affect the validity of any ordinance otherwise
regularly adopted.
  f. Where the council is authorized to act by a resolution,
such resolution shall be read in full, unless, after reading of
the title thereof, a further reading thereof is waived by a
unanimous vote of the councilmen present in the manner pro-
vided in subsection (a) hereof for waiver of reading of ordi-
nances in full."

            "Section 613.    Ordinances—Amendment.
   No ordinance shall be revised, re-enacted or amended by
reference to its title only; but the ordinance may be revised
or re-enacted, or the section, sections, or subsections thereof to
be amended, or the new section, sections, or subsections to be
added thereto shall be set forth at length as to the particular
section, sections, or subsection to be so revised, re-enacted or
adopted, and adopted in the method provided in Section 611
of this Charter. No ordinance or section or subsection thereof
shall be repealed except by an ordinance adopted in the man-
ner provided in this Charter, provided that an ordinance, sec-
tion or subsection thereof may be repealed by reference to the
number of the ordinance, section or subsection and to the
title of the ordinance or section."
