                                (1)
    GOVERNOR'S
REORGANIZATION PLANS

        1969
 Reorganization Message of



RONALD REAGAN


  Governor of     California




      Transmitted to the

 CALIFORNIA LEGISLATURE

  Wednesday, March 5, 1969
To the Members of the Legislature of California;
   In submitting last year's Eeorganization Plan No. 1 of 1968
for consideration by the Legislature I called attention to some of
the factors of change which alter the circumstances of government
such as growth, technology, management techniques, and changes
in public policy, and I pointed out that organizational response
to pressures for change can result in a proliferation of unco-
ordinated government activities.
   A major purpose of last year's plan was to establish a more
manageable structure in the Executive Branch, with four major
agencies and a small, working cabinet. Another was improvement
of communications with all levels of government on matters of
major objectives, policies, and programs through proper use of
Agency Secretaries as advisors to the Governor and representa-
tives of his authority in Agency matters.
   These purposes have been achieved and the basic, reorganized
structure of our Executive Branch has proven to be sound, work-
able, and effective.
   There were other objectives stated as well, such as bringing
groups of programs and services into clear, coordinated rela-
tionship to each other, insuring a more continuous and uniform
review of program performance, and highlighting overlapping
and obsolete functions for necessary restructuring. Reorganiza-
tion was one means of attaining such objectives. A companion
means was the institution of program budgeting for all State
Government activities, a form of budget presentation which
focuses on goals, in-depth analysis of alternatives and measure-
ment of achievement of objectives. These are essential elements
of decisions by policy makers in the difficult task of allocating
resources among competing needs. The combination of pro-
gram budgeting and the continuing work to secure the organiza-
tion objectives will lead directly to the identification of many
reorganization requirements as we are able to identify programs
and analyze program goals.

                               (3)
                              ~_ 4 —

   However, there is a second reason for focusing attention oh
these objectives. In any human endeavor of the size and
scope of California state government it is never possible to say
that these objectives have been achieved for all possible cases.
Rather, they are continuing objectives and an organization of
such dimensions needs continuous improvement. This is never
a matter of change for its own sake, but we need to be sure, at
all times, that our reasons for leaving any organization structure
unchanged are as valid and sound as our reasons for altering
those which we do change.
   Under the authority of the constitutional amendment approved
by the voters in 1966, the Legislature in 1967, in Senate Bill 296,
empowered the Governor to reorganize the Executive Branch,
subject to review by the Legislature. In Government Code Sec-
tion 12080.1 the Legislature stated its purposes in granting this
authority. Among them were:
    "To group, consolidate and coordinate agencies and functions
  thereof as nearly as possible according to major purposes;
    To reduce the number of agencies by consolidating those
  having similar functions under a single head and to abolish
  such agencies or functions thereof as may not be necessary for
  the efficient operation of state government;
    To eliminate overlapping and duplication of effort."

   These objectives are an excellent incentive to the Executive
Branch to examine its organization continuously. However, under
Government Code Section 12081.2 the Governor's authority to
submit reorganization plans to the Legislature expires on Decem-
ber 31,1969.
   I believe it is essential that the Executive Branch have both the
continuing incentive and the authority to examine its organiza-
tion structure and components and to recommend changes com-
patible with changing circumstances and with the emergence of
new needs. Therefore, I have requested the introduction of legis-
lation in the current session which will continue the Governor's
                              — 5 —

authority to transmit reorganization plans under Government
Code Section 12080.2. The extension of this authority is one of
the most important and significant reorganization actions that
can be taken for the benefit of the people of California. I strongly
urge your favorable consideration of this legislation.
   In addition to those already quoted, Government Code Sec-
tion 12080.1 also states these purposes of the Legislature:
       "To promote the better execution of the laws, the more
    effective management of the executive and administrative
    branch of the state government and of its agencies and
    functions and the expeditious administration of the public
    business;
      To reduce expenditures and promote economy to the fullest
    extent practicable consistent with the efficient operation of
    state government;
      To increase the efficiency of the operation of the state
    government to the fullest extent practicable; . . . ."

  These are purposes with which this Administration is in full
accord, and they are a foundation for actions included in these
reorganization proposals. There are, however, three other bases
for action which have been expressed previously by this Adminis-
tration as part of its philosophy of government. The influence of
these beliefs is also evident and therefore they are clearly stated
here. They are:
  1. There should be a conscious effort on the part of each level
     of government to keep government as small as is possible
     and consistent with the basic obligation of meeting the real
     needs of the people.
  2. Higher levels of government should continually search for
     opportunities to return governmental functions to local gov-
     ernment levels and devolve enabling duties, responsibilities
     and power to local government for functions it can per-
     form equally well or better.
                                — 6 —

   3. All levels of government should seek to enlist the interest,
      concern, and active participation of the private sector to
      solve public problems. The private sector should be en-
      couraged to become a joint partner or even a friendly
      competitor with government in acting to achieve the social
      goals of the entire citizenry.

     The actions proposed in the reorganization plans of 1969
  reflect the spirit of the stated purposes of the Legislature
  and of these beliefs. They constitute more than a management
  improvement plan. They are a thrust toward the future, a thought-
  ful attempt to re-direct some aspects of government in ways which
  will better serve the needs of the people. I t is in the same spirit
  that they are submitted for your review.
     The first reorganization action I wish to call to your attention
  is the action which has already been taken to return to local
  governmental jurisdiction the San Francisco Port Authority.
  The operation of the Port was assumed by State Government
  in the latter part of the last century, and since that time had
 been a separate function of State Government, responsible only
 to the Governor. This had also been the only state operated port.
 The State did undertake extensive development of 8 miles of
 waterfront lands from Aquatic Park to the China Basin includ-
 ing piers, Fisherman's Wharf and the Belt Railway. However,
 as other California ports were developed and presented compe-
 tition for San Francisco's port business, this state controlled
function was not always as responsive to local needs as a city
 operated port might have been. Therefore, despite the immense
monetary value of the Port Lands today, and in the firm belief
that ownership and operation of a port is properly a local rather
than a State function, I supported the proposal to return
the Port of San Francisco without requiring "payment of fair
value" or similar compensation by the City and County to the
State. This is a significant reversal of the modern trend of each
level of government which has consistently sought increased
powers, duties, revenues and spending authorities.
  In a similar manner, and for the same reasons of returning
to local government functions which properly belong to them
I am recommending elimination of the following functions from
State Government, effective on January 1, 1971;
    Board of Pilot Commissioners and the Pilotage Rate Com-
    mittee for the Bays of San Francisco, San Pablo and Suisun
    Board of Pilot Commissioners for Humboldt Bay and Bar
    Board of Pilot Commissioners for the Harbor of San Diego
    Board of Harbor Commissioners for Humboldt Bay

   The effective date of these actions provides ample time for
local assumption of these responsibilities.
   We have also initiated discussions with the Board of Directors
of the Museum of Science and Industry, to explore the feasibility
of transferring the operation of the Museum to the appropriate
local jurisdiction.
   Voluntary participation of the private sector in government
matters and in developing independent solutions to social prob-
lems has long been a traditional part of the American way of
life. It has spanned a broad spectrum of activities, from
volunteer fire companies and citizens' committees to the en-
dowment of great universities and cultural institutions and the
formation of immense foundations for research and social im-
provement. The motivation of the individual citizens of America
to form associations, independent institutions for social pur-
poses, was seen by Alexis de Tocqueville as long ago as the
1830 's as a remarkable and almost unique characteristic of
American life. This impulse to band together outside the sphere
of politics for purposes of building, and not of tearing down,
is still very much alive. It can be seen today in many places
where ordinary citizens are at work together in their own self-
interest. Sometimes they are joined by common interest in a
field of work, a form of recreation, or the threat of a mutually
shared problem. Sometimes they come from totally different
fields and interests, joined only by a shared sense of humanity
                               — 8 _

  and a common recognition of a need to be met and satisfied.
  This impulse to engage in constructive independent action
  should be supported and encouraged wherever it arises, in all
  contexts, whether large or small.
     The people of California have shown repeatedly that they
  will respond to stated needs on an ad hoc basis, as they did in
 the case of the Governor's Survey on Efficiency and Cost Con-
  trol, and the commission which helped the Department of Cor-
 porations rewrite the corporation code. These ad hoc groups
 are immediately disbanded when the stated purpose has been
 achieved. On the other hand, statutorily established boards,
 commissions and functions exhibit a tendency to perpetuate
 themselves even beyond any reasonable need or usefulness. This
 appears to be based upon an assumption that the Legislature fore-
 saw a continuing need and that self-perpetuation would be the
 only way to fulfill that expectation. Reorganization Plan No. 1
 of 1969 eliminates many boards and commissions in the firm
 belief that their expertise is available to State Government on
 call or that, in some cases, independently organized bodies will
 perform as effectively as permanent statutory agencies.
    I hope that a resurgence of independent action will permit
 additional reductions in government activities and will present
valid alternatives to the continuing tendency of government to
 expand its powers and authorities.
    There are several major departmental reorganizations this
year which continue at the department level the kind of re-
structuring done last year at the cabinet level, consolidating
functions for more effective use of resources, better communica-
tion of policy decisions, and better coordination of ideas and
programs as well as other reasons.
    In the field of revenue administration there are certain obvious
criteria that should be met. The taxpaying public should be able
to identify, simply and immediately, the tax collecting agency
with which it must deal in relation to any tax matter. Tax
administration should be straightforward and direct, as a prin-
cipal responsibility of the Governor, consistent with the opera-
                              — 9—
tion of other state agencies under the Governor's jurisdiction.
Authority for judgments in tax appeals should be distinct and
separate from authorities for tax administration. Information
reported to the state government for various tax administration
purposes should be as simple and as uniform as possible, and
should lend itself readily to preparation by the tax paying
public, comparison, and cross-checking. Finally, tax administra-
tion should be organized and conducted in a sound, business-like
fashion which takes maximum advantage of economies of spe-
cialization and scale, which achieves maximum utilization of
equipment and facilities, which insures the best possible use
of manpower skills and resources, and which performs its tasks
efficiently as well as effectively.
   The organization structure for revenue collection in California
totally fails to satisfy any one of those criteria. While the sev-
eral revenue collection agencies are to be commended on their
individual operations, the very fact that they are individual and
separate insures that these goals cannot be achieved. No organ-
ization structure which has evolved over time through a series of
immediate responses to current crises can possibly operate as
efficiently and effectively as an organization which is deliberately
designed with the total problem and ultimate objectives con-
stantly in view.
   None of these observations originate with this Administration;
all have been made many times before. I n fact, every study of
tax administration that has been made in California has recom-
mended consolidation and integration of revenue functions for
the past 40 years. Since 1965 there has been universal agreement
among the major revenue collecting functions themselves that
significant economies can be achieved through consolidation of
tax programs and integration of tax collection functions. This
concept has been supported by governors of both parties, by the
Board of Equalization, by the Franchise Tax Board and its Ex-
ecutive Officer, by the State Controller, by the Director of Fi-
nance, by the Legislative Analyst, by the Commission on Califor-
nia State Government Organization and Economy (the "Little
                              — 10 —
Hoover" Commission), by the Assembly Interim Committee on
Government Organization, by independent management consult-
ants, by the Governor's Task Force on Efficiency and Cost Con-
trol, by respected and influential members of the Legislature
representing both parties—and yet, nothing happens.
   Certainly one of the most important reorganization proposals
you will be considering this year will be legislation to consolidate
and integrate the revenue administration functions of the Fran-
chise Tax Board, the Board of Equalization and the Office of the
State Controller. The legislation should propose a single Depart-
ment of Revenue, under the administration of a Director ap-
pointed by and responsible to the Governor and removable for
cause by the Legislature. I t should also provide for the estab-
lishment of a separate Tax Appeals Board, one not composed
of the executives heading the functions which are party to the
conflict, but fairly constituted to judge all aspects of tax matters.
   Since this proposal contemplates elimination of both the Fran-
chise Tax Board and the Board of Equalization, as presently
constituted, implementation will also require both statutory
changes and a constitutional amendment. Additionally, the
function of inheritance tax appraisal should remain with the
State Controller until the necessary reforms in this func-
tion have been accomplished. For these reasons, and to permit
reasonable time for administrative adjustments, the legislation
should specify a future effective date allowing sufficient time for
all necessary planning and implementation to insure a smooth
transition.
   There is no single item of reorganization proposed this year
which will have a greater long-term significance for California's
current and future citizens than this matter of tax administration.
I urge you to overcome any and all obstacles in carrying out this
organizational reform which has been so uniformly supported
and so repeatedly thwarted.
   The newly created Department of Human Resources Develop-
ment is a singularly successful example of cooperation and under-
standing between the Legislature and the Executive Branch.
                              — 11 —
The Department was established last year by Assembly Bill No.
1463, as an extension of Reorganization Plan No. 1 of 1968 and
aimed at getting the chronically unemployed and underemployed
into the mainstream of American productivity. This Administra-
tion has made great strides in effecting the planning and organiz-
ational actions necessary to carry out the intent of the Legislature.
   Both the Legislature and the Executive Branch faced up to
the many problems caused by the proliferation and fragmentation
of federally assisted state programs, and this joint effort pro-
duced some unique and innovative approaches to one of the State's
most urgent problems—successful employment for the unem-
ployed and underemployed. The principal provisions and goals
of this major reorganization are:
  1. To consolidate, to the maximum extent possible, all the func-
     tions related to job training and placement services in order
     that a unified, coordinated system might be designed and acti-
     vated which will remove employable people from public de-
     pendency and otherwise assist the unemployed in obtaining
     steady employment commensurate with their abilities and
     skills.
  2. To channel the numerous, scattered funds available for job
     training and placement services into a single Manpower
     Development Fund to be administered by the Department
     of Human Resources Development in order to provide flexi-
     bility and facilitate the directed use of funds in accordance
     with specifically established priorities of need and policy
     goals.
  3. To require the Department of Human Resources Develop-
     ment to submit an annual program budget including not
     only its own expenditures but also expenditures proposed
     to be made under any related program or by any other
     state agency for services incidental to those of the Depart-
     ment, thereby giving visibility to all aspects of the total
     effort.
                             — 12 —
  4. To require other departments and agencies to contract with
     the Department to provide services which it requires and
     to otherwise make available to the Department all author-
     ized services to eligible persons.
  5. To authorize the Department to make maximum use of
     total community resources, to contract for both public and
     private job training and placement programs, and to enlist
     the full support of private industry in achieving the De-
     partment's goals.
  6. To establish a program approach of an unbroken sequence
     of services for eligible persons based on individual need
     including specific goals and objectives, development of a
     training and employment plan, a continuing review of
     progress and a measurement of final achievement through
     periodic postemployment followup.
  7. To establish a new kind of civil servant, the Job Agent,
     who will establish a close, personal relationship and inter-
     action with each individual whom he serves. This relation-
     ship will extend not only through the determination of
     needs, development of a training and employment plan,
     procurement of training services and eventual placement.
     It will also continue for 18 months following employment
     to secure the success of the individual in achieving self-
     dependence, to ascertain for the first time on a formal
     basis the effectiveness of the plan used in each individual
     case, and to serve as a means of measuring the perform-
     ance of the Job Agent himself.
  8. To authorize a method of compensation for Job Agents
     which incorporates an incentive feature by means of which
     outstanding performance and success may be given recog-
     nition in the form of higher earnings.
   This reorganization, in addition, continues the successful func-
tions of the Governor's Job Training and Placement Council in
the form of the Job Training and Development Services Ad-
visory Board which will work in close cooperation with the new
                             — 13 —
Department, studying statewide problems of job training and
placement, advising the Director, reviewing periodic progress
reports and reporting suggestions and recommendations annually
to the Director, the Governor and the Legislature. Statutory
establishment of this Board obviates the need for several other
activities which are eliminated in the Plan. These are the Com-
mission on Manpower, Automation and Technology, the State
Manpower Advisory Committee, and the State Advisory Council
in the Department of Employment. All pertinent responsibilities
of these activities will be incorporated in the new Advisory
Board.
   In order to provide sufficient time for an orderly transition
and necessary organization planning and adjustments, the statute
provides that the act will become operative at such time as is
recommended by the Director of the Department of Human Re-
sources Development, but not later than January 1, 1970. I am
pleased to report that the Director of the Department has been
appointed, transfers are being made, new structures are being
established and staffed, and I am confident that the Department
will be fully operative well in advance of the mandated date.
   As part of our reorganization effort, this year we will endeavor
to submit legislative proposals which will represent some
necessary first steps toward a more consolidated, integrated
organization to deal with the public aspects of health. We have
investigated activities related to health and have learned that
rapid technological change, increased spending for health related
purposes, and improved abilities to identify and deal with health
problems have, in turn, generated a need for coordination and
contributed to problems of overlap, fragmentation and confusion
in the health field. In recent years there has been a growing
recognition, at all levels of government, of the multiplicity of
problems which pose current and potential threats to public
 health. Causes of concern are as varied as: planning for adequate
 hospital facilities, public and private, to serve a growing popu-
 lation, reversing the trend of environmental pollution, identify-
 ing and correcting conditions which breed pests and disease,
 containing and eliminating threatened epidemics and communi-
                              — 14 —
 cable diseases, providing for health maintenance of all citizens
 of all ages, to name but a few. A great many separate efforts
 have been undertaken to deal with those threats to public health.
 Annual expenditures from tax sources at all levels of govern-
 ment for health and health related services in California alone
 have been estimated at over 2 billion dollars. This fragmented
 response, at federal, state, and local levels must now be pulled
 together in a manner which will reduce or eliminate overlapping
 functions, provide for better planning and coordination of the
 total research effort, achieve closer organizational ties between
 medical, rehabilitative, and social services, improve program
 planning for health, and simplify the delivery of health and
 related services to the person served. The federal government's
 present emphasis is on coordination between programs and insti-
 tutions, in each state, to achieve effective, comprehensive health
 planning.
   Our objectives are similar, with emphasis on greater visibility
 of the whole health field with all its ramifications, a more easily
 understood structure facilitating communication with all levels
 of government as well as with the private sector, and to gain
maximum public benefit from resources expended. This maxi-
mum benefit will be achieved through adequate planning which
will eliminate program overlaps and fragmentation of efforts.
"We plan to concentrate efforts and funding at locations which
will produce the best results. Further, comprehensive planning
will insure that limited manpower and technological skills are
applied where they are most needed in accordance with sound
priorities.
   Your thoughtful judgment and support will be necessary if
these goals are to be won.
   The ocean is California's last major undeveloped resource.
We are only at the threshold of knowledge of the sea itself and
of the development and use of its vast resources. The Santa
Barbara offshore deep water oil drilling tragedy emphasizes our
need to know a great deal more about the characteristics of the
ocean floor and the means of developing this resource without
                             — 15 —
injury to our matchless environment. Scientific research in
California by Scripps Institute, the United States Navy, private
corporations and other organizations already has made this state
a recognized world leader in the field of oceanography. Yet we
have not effectively addressed ourselves to the optimum, planned
development of our ocean for recreation, for the protection
of its environment as natural sanctuaries, for trade, for increas-
ing scientific knowledge, and for extracting and harvesting its
resources, each in ways that do not risk its destruction for any
of those purposes.
   Ocean technology is expanding at an extremely rapid rate.
Man-in-the-sea programs, experimental submersible vehicles,
fixed foundation platforms and stable floating platforms are
daily proving man's new-found abilities to work with, on, and
in the sea. California's opportunities are unique in the combina-
tion of its extensive coastline exposure to the ocean, its moderate
climate and weather conditions, its orientation to research, and
its highly developed technological industries. Within State gov-
ernment certain actions have been taken toward comprehensive
planning.
   I am proposing, in Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1969, a
Department of Navigation and Ocean Development to provide
the necessary structure of government so that a Comprehensive
Ocean Area Plan for California can become a reality. The
Department of Navigation and Ocean Development would have
the continuing responsibility for implementation of this plan, a
vital responsibility which does not now exist within State
government.
   In order to harness the collective resources of State govern-
ment, I established the Interagency Council on Ocean Resources,
composed of representatives of those agencies of government
with interests in California's coastline and knowledge to con-
tribute to its development.
   Because of his interest in and knowledge of the ocean and
the vast opportunities it contains for the enjoyment of the
people and the economy of the State, I am again asking the
                              — 16 —

 Lieutenant Governor, as my designee, to assume the leadership
 in the effort to assure that we have an orderly plan for the
 recreational and commercial development of the ocean. His in-
 terest, knowledge and leadership in this subject, as a member
 of the Congress, give him unique qualifications for this task,
    In 1967, we established the California Advisory Commission
 on Coastal and Marine Resources by an act of the California
 Legislature, with responsibility to report recommendations to
 the Governor and the Legislature. This Commission brings to
 bear on the planned development of the ocean the resources
 and expertise of the private sector together with California's
 rich educational resources. The Commission can serve in an
 advisory capacity to the Department of Navigation and Ocean
 Development, thus establishing the necessary interaction be-
 tween ideas, workable planning and the combined resources of
 State government.
    I have requested an internal reorganization within the De-
 partment of Fish and Game to permit that department to work
 in close coordination and cooperation with the new department
 and to bring its considerable resources to bear in developing
the comprehensive plan. This will be done without adversely
 affecting the constitutional and statutory responsibilities of the
Department of Fish and Game.
    The Department of Navigation and Ocean Development would
continue the functions of harbor development, boating safety, and
boating regulations from the Department of Harbors and Wa-
tercraft. It would have authority over all ocean tidelands and
coastal submerged lands except for the matter of minerals which
would remain the responsibility of the State Lands Commission.
It would assume all responsibilities for boating facility planning
and design currently split between the Department of Harbors
and Watercraft and the Office of Architecture and Construction.
I t would be responsible for beach erosion control programs,
ocean-oriented mapping, ocean-oriented power plant sites and
ocean-oriented nuclear development.
   Registration of privately owned pleasure craft and other un-
documented vessels would become the responsibility of the De-
                                       — 17 —
partment of Motor Vehicles, taking maximum advantage of its
highly developed computer system, widespread facilities and
efficient procedures for registration. Records of boat ownerships
would be maintained electronically on high speed devices which
would provide immediate responses to inquiries from the new
Department, from law enforcement activities, or others.
   The Department of Navigation and Ocean Development will be
the key to California's ocean future. Its formation now will in-
sure that California will remain in the vanguard of oceanog-
raphy, marine research, ocean conservation and ocean resources
development among the states of the nation and the nations of
the world. It not only will guarantee the wisest use of this greatest
and last resource for Californians, it also will insure that Cali-
fornia will be both leader and helper to all of its Pacific Ocean
Basin neighbors as the exploration and uses of the "inner space"
of the seas advances into the next century.
   Reorganization Plan No. 3 * will provide an opportunity to con-
duct more efficiently the business of the Department of Profes-
sional and Vocational Standards.
   Private citizens with problems involving licensed and regulated
businesses or professions have frequently had trouble finding the
right state agency to provide the help they need. To eliminate
this difficulty, the plan proposes to change the name of the De-
partment of Professional and Vocational Standards to the more
descriptive: Department of Business and Professional Licensing.
   Other changes in this department are similarly directed toward
making the structures and practices of the 40 boards, bureaus,
commissions, and committees more uniform and readily under-
standable.
   The Department will then be able to operate more efficiently
and provide a greater responsiveness in maintaining the protec-
tion of the public of California.
   In preparing for this year's reorganization, I asked all depart-
ment heads to examine the boards, commissions, and committees
under their jurisdiction and to recommend for elimination any
which are inactive, unnecessary, unproductive, or engaged in
* Re-referred to Committee on Governmental Organization June 27 (See Assembly Journal, page
    5725).
    132—1954
                             — 18 —

activities which can properly be assumed by another function of
government, a local level of government, or by the private sector.
As a direct result I am recommending elimination of many
boards, commissions, and committees in Reorganization Plan
No. 1 of 1969. Many of these entities involve significant expendi-
tures for employed personnel. Many others have had funds budg-
eted and allocated for reimbursement of members' travel costs
and other expenditures. By virtue of their number, all of them
have added to the complexity and confusion of government. The
proliferation of boards, commissions and committees frequently
interferes with the principle of clear authority and responsi-
bility, clearly assigned, and with accountability for results. This
administration will seek continuously to apply that principle to
government functions and to avoid eroding it by spreading au-
thority so thinly through so many boards and commissions that
no one can finally be held accountable. Where advice and guid-
ance to government functions is needed on a short term basis we
intend to trust California's citizens to respond to the State's
needs, as they have done so often and so well. In addition to the
outstanding work of the Governor's Survey on Efficiency and
Cost Control previously mentioned there have been numerous
contributions by groups temporarily appointed for specific tasks,
such as the excellent work of the committee appointed to draft
the Corporate Securities Law of 1968. These kinds of ad hoc
appointments will be continued.
  Where statutory functions are established for an indeter-
minate period, I will encourage the Legislature, as it has done
occasionally in the past, to include provisions for abolition of
those functions by the Governor when the services are no longer
required.
  I have mentioned previously some activities which are being
shifted to local levels of government, such as the San Francisco
Port Authority and several Boards of Pilot Commissioners.
  There are five functions which are currently performed volun-
tarily by the private sector or which can be obtained by State
government on an ad hoc basis. They are the Program Advisory
                             — 19 —

Committee to the Consumer Counsel, the United Spanish War
Veterans Commission, the Television Advisory Committee, the
Public Library Development Board, and the Advisory Council
on Atomic Energy Development and Radiation Protection. Re-
organization Plan No. 1 proposes elimination of these functions
as statutory bodies.
   Thirteen functions have been identified which can be trans-
ferred or absorbed by other agencies which are more appropriate
locations. Elimination of some of these functions as separate en-
tities will also involve the obtaining of advice and counsel regard-
ing specific problems on an ad hoc basis. Organizations proposed
for elimination as separate entities with functions transferred to
or absorbed by other agencies are :
   1. Capitol Building and Planning Commission
   2. Technical Advisory Committee to the Director of Com-
      merce
   3. Districts Securities Commission
   4. Office of Atomic Energy Development and Radiation Pro-
      tection
   5. Planning Advisory Committee
   6. Commission on Manpower, Automation and Technology
   7. State Manpower Advisory Committee
   8. Advisory Hospital Council
   9. State Advisory Council to the Department of Employment
  10. Cannery Inspection Board
  11. Narcotic Rehabilitation Advisory Council
  12. California Delinquency Prevention Commission
  13. Marine Research Committee
  I am proposing that seven functions be eliminated entirely for
a variety of reasons. The Governor's Council has become large
and cumbersome, and is not required because of the new use of
                             — 20 —

the Governor's Cabinet as an effective means of communication.
The work of the Colorado Boundary Commission has been com-
pleted. Elimination of the California-Nevada Interstate Compact
Commission and the Goose Lake Compact Commission is pro-
posed with an effective date no later than January 1, 1971, thus
providing ample time for completion of their assigned responsi-
bilities.
   The State Soil Conservation Advisory Board, the Coordinat-
ing Council on Alcohol Problems, and the Atomic Energy Co-
ordinating Committee are comprised primarily of representatives
of State departments who are State employees and are available
for consultation as needed. Therefore, I propose their elimination
as statutory functions. Finally, it has been determined that
the activities of the New Car Dealers Policy and Appeals Board
are not required as a statutory State function.
   We have not directed our attention solely to opportunities to
reduce, consolidate and eliminate functions from State govern-
ment. We have also recognized the need to extend required func-
tions beyond their scheduled expiration dates where this action
is warranted and justified. For example, the law creating the
Bay Conservation and Development Commission will expire in
October, 1969. The Commission has recommended a master plan
for the Bay, to be administered by a regional agency represent-
ing the interests of the local people and the local governments
concerned. I wholeheartedly support the idea of local govern-
ment responsibility, on a regional basis, to direct the orderly
development of the Bay, permitting appropriate municipal and
industrial uses but only in a manner which will preserve and
protect its shores and guarantee that recreational and esthetic
use of the Bay is not jeopardized. However, since it may take
some time to establish this local and regional authority, in order
to insure that San Francisco Bay will not, for even a single day,
be left unprotected and subject to filling at the whim of any
individual, I urge once again that the permit-granting powers
of the Bay Conservation and Development Commission be con-
tinued until local control has been firmly established.
                               — 21 —
   I also urge extension of the P r o g r a m for Rehabilitation of
Alcoholics and the assignment of responsibility for this program
in the Department of Rehabilitation. Rehabilitation of the alco-
holic is one of the most difficult problems of our society. I t is also
one of the most tragic of losses to self, family, and society, pre-
cisely because rehabilitation can be achieved and the alcoholic can
regain his place within his family and his society. Alcoholics are
estimated to be the fourth largest disability group in the nation.
The significant achievements already recorded by the Rehabilita-
tion program present strong evidence that this problem, once
thought to be generally beyond hope of solution, can be attacked
successfully. F o r example, more than 1,000 alcoholics were re-
habilitated in 1967-68, and current projections indicate twice
that number will be reached in the current year 1968-69. An-
nual earnings of rehabilitated alcoholics increased by over $2,-
400,000. A representative sample of rehabilitated alcoholics
showed that after six months:
    51% had been totally abstinent
    21% more had drunk in such moderation as to represent
        no significant problem
    85% had no marital difficulties attributed to alcoholism
    89% had no job difficulties such as job loss or disciplinary
        action
    94% had no work days lost due to alcoholism
    96% had no hospitalization due to alcoholism
    93% had no arrests due to alcoholism

  As I mentioned in connection with the J o b Agent in the
Department of Human Resources Development, procedures to
follow up rehabilitated persons and obtain a true measure of
performance over a period of time are being applied also in
this program.
  A careful analysis of the existing separation of functions and
responsibilities along with consideration of program perform-
ance has led to the recommendation to consolidate responsibilities
                             — 22 —

for alcoholic rehabilitation in the Department of Rehabilitation.
   The actions proposed in Reorganization P l a n No. 1 of 1969 on
boards and commissions will directly reduce expenditures for
state government. However, these direct budget reductions do
not tell the whole story, since they do not reflect the administra-
tive and other costs of various supporting activities which must
process forms, handle requests and travel expense claims, issue
checks and do the many other jobs necessary to support activities
which may themselves have limited budgets or no budgets. While
it is important to insure that money is not spent unnecessarily,
it is even more important to see that money which is spent is
spent wisely on the highest priorities and that the optimum bene-
fits are obtained. This is the basis of Reorganization Plan No. 2
of 1969 and is the major focus of our continuing reorganization
effort and the underlying motivation for all the changes.
   State government will, at best, continue to be an enterprise of
vast proportions and great complexity. I appreciate the oppor-
tunity that this Administration has had to work with the Cali-
fornia Legislature, the Commission on California State Govern-
ment Organization and Economy, and all organizations of State
Government to simplify organization structures, improve com-
munication, improve the visibility of programs and activities and
seek more efficient operations and more effective solutions to our
pressing problems.
   W i t h your help we shall continue our efforts to balance the
demands of tomorrow's ideals with today's realities; we shall
seek continually to improve the circumstances of life and the
opportunities for self-development of all of our citizens; we shall
conserve our resources, applying them wisely for the greatest
benefit; we shall plan for success and not merely hope for i t ; we
shall propose and institute change where change is needed and
justified, but not for the sake of novelty or the momentary
glamour of a new approach; we shall make judicious use of the
most effective new techniques along with all that is best in the
traditional practices: and we shall guarantee our State's future
by the soundness with which we build the foundations of that
future today.
                             _   23 —

  At the Legislature's request and with the cooperation of the
Legislative Counsel the statutory language required to reflect the
changes made by the Reorganization Plans of 1969 is being pre-
pared and will follow shortly.

                           (3)
               GOVERNOR'S MESSAGE
   In accordance with Section 12080.2 of the Gov-
ernment Code, I am submitting Reorganization
Plan No. 1 of 1969 for review by the Legislature.
It is also being reviewed by the Commission on
California State Government Organization and
Economy. I have found each reorganization ac-
tion included in this Plan to be in the public
interest.
   The actions proposed in this Plan will increase
efficiency, save the taxpayers money, eliminate
unnecessary units of the Executive Branch, and
consolidate like functions to increase coordination
and decrease overlap and duplication.
   This is by no means all of the reorganizations
I am proposing. In my message of March 5, 1969,
I outlined this and several other major and nec-
essary changes. This Plan is an important ele-
ment in the continuing process of updating our
State Government. With your support I am sure
this Plan will prove to be a constructive first step
in modernizing the maze of boards and commis-
sions we find in State Government.

              REORGANIZATION ACTIONS
1. The Program Advisory Committee to the Con-
   sumer Counsel is eliminated. The statutory au-
   thority providing for the creation of such a
   committee is rescinded.
                   Explanatory Material:
    The function of this Committee, program and policy
  advice to the Consumer Counsel, is now being performed
  voluntarily by the private sector at no expense to the
  State. The statutory language authorizing the establish-
  ment of this Committee by Executive Order is no longer
  needed.
  Statutes Suspended:
       Government Code Section 12057
  Statutory Amendments and Additions:
       None

2. The United Spanish War Veterans Commission is
    eliminated.
                    Explanatory Material:
     This Commission of five members appointed by the
   Governor was created in 1957 to assist in the maintenance
   of California as an active unit of the National Encamp-
   ment of the United Spanish "War Veterans. Inasmuch as
   funding was not provided in 1968-69, it is apparent that
   State funding is no longer needed. Private organizations
   can support this activity. This saves the General Fund
   $3,600.
   Statutes Suspended:
        Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 1300) of Divi-
        sion 6 of the Military and Veterans Code
   Statutory Amendments and Additions:
        None

3. The Television Advisory Committee and the posi-
   tion of Television Coordinator are eliminated and
   the functions, authorities and responsibilities
   transferred to the Department of General Serv-
   ices.
                   Explanatory Material:
     The Committee provides advice and guidance to the
  Television Coordinator in the performance of his duties
  as the primary coordinator of the activities of the various
  public and nonprofit agencies concerned with television
                               — 8 —
     for educational purposes. It has been determined that the
     Coordinator's functions can be absorbed by the Depart-
     ment of General Services with a resultant savings to the
     General Fund of $50,322. Advice and guidance are neces-
     sary in this field and will be obtained on an ad hoc basis
     at no expense to the State.
     Statutes Suspended:
          Article 8.5 (commencing with Section 8871) of Chap-
          ter 6, Division 7, Part 2 of the Education Code
     Statutory Amendments and Additions:
          Government Code Sections 14656, 14716, 14716.1,
          14716.2, and 14716.3

 4. The Capitol Building and Planning Commission
    is eliminated and its functions, authorities and
    responsibilities transferred to the Department of
    General Services.
                    Explanatory Material:
        The primary functions of this Commission are to estab-
     lish a master plan for the orderly development of future
     State buildings in the Capitol area of the City of Sacra-
     mento and the County of Sacramento and to formulate
     and carry out a long-range master plan for improvement
     of the Capitol Mall. These functions can be absorbed by
     the Department of General Services with advice and
     counsel obtained when specific problems need resolution.
     This will be on an ad hoc basis at no expenses to the
     State with a resultant savings to the General Fund of
     $2,250.
     Statutes Suspended:
          Chapter 2.8 (commencing with Section 8160) of Di-
          vision 1 of Title 2 of the Government Code
     Statutory Amendments and Additions:
          Government Code Sections 8160-8169.5 and 14657

 5. The statutory authority for the Governor to ap-
    point a Technical Advisory Committee to advise
    the Director of Commerce is eliminated. The Cal-
    ifornia World Trade Authority is renamed the
    California Industry and World Trade Commission
    and its membership is changed to fifteen mem-
    bers appointed by and serving at the Governor's
    pleasure.*
* Changes provided for in this sentence were accomplished by legislative
    action. See Stats. 1969, Ch. 1161.
                                 — 9 —

                       Explanatory Material:
       The Economic Development Agency has been consoli-
     dated into the Department of Commerce and the technical
     advisory functions needed can be provided by the Cali-
     fornia Industry and AVorld Trade Commission.
       To carry out more accurately the purposes of the De-
     partment of Commerce, the California World Trade Au-
     thority should be renamed to the California Industry and
     World Trade Commission. Fifteen members will provide
     a broad perspective on the complex geographic, industrial,
     business and world trade activities of our State.
     Statutory Amendments and Additions:
          Government Code Sections 8320, 8321, 8350-8353,
          8356-8360, 8370-8373, 8380-8387, and 8400-8402

 6.* The Districts Securities Commission is elimi-
    nated and its functions, authorities and respon-
    sibilities transferred to the Department of Corpo-
    rations.
                        Explanatory Material:
        This Commission regulates some long-term debts of cer-
     tain water districts as described in the Water Code. These
     are primarily irrigation districts, water districts and water
     storage districts; there are approximately 265 such dis-
     tricts. However some 2,000 more districts apparently have
     the choice of whether to have their bonds certified by this
     Commission and have not found this to be necessary or
     desirable. Examples of such districts are drainage dis-
     tricts, public utility districts and reclamation districts.
        The general financial activities of the Department of
     Corporations are very similar to those performed by the
     Commission in a specialized field.
        The Department of Corporations can absorb the activi-
     ties of the Districts Securities Commission without in-
     creasing its budget. This will permit lowering the fees
     charged the various water districts by the Commission.
     These savings can be passed on to the consumer.
     Statutes   Suspended:
          Water Code Sections 20015-20023.
     Statutory Amendments and Additions:
          Water Code Sections 20000, 20001, 20003, 20004,
          20024-20033, 20040-20048, 20051-20053, 20061,
          20080-20087, 20100-20104, and 20106.

 7. The Office of Atomic Energy Development and
    Radiation Protection is eliminated and its func-
    tions, authorities and responsibilities transferred
    to the Resources Agency.

9. The Advisory Council on Atomic Energy Develop-
   ment and Radiation Protection is eliminated.
                    Explanatory Material:
     This Council was established to evaluate the programs
  of the various State agencies and to make recommenda-
  tions to the Governor regarding State policy in the field
  of atomic energy development and radiation protection.
     The Council has been relatively inactive and it is un-
  necessary to continue it on a statutory basis. If evaluation
  and policy recommendations become necessary, they can
  be obtained on an ad hoc basis at no cost to the State.
  The expenditures of this Council have been part of the

   budget appropriation for the Office of Nuclear Energy and

10. The Colorado River Boundary Commission is
    eliminated.
                Explanatory Material:
     As the result of the work of this Commission a common
   boundary line with respect to the Colorado River has
   been established between California and Arizona and a
   compact ratified by both states and the Congress of the
   United States. This completes the primary objective of
   the Commission, and it is no longer necessary.
   Statutes Suspended:
        Chapter 1693 of the Statutes of 1953
   Statutory Amendments     and    Additions:
        None

11. The California-Nevada Interstate Compact Com-
    mission is eliminated effective when the compact
    has been ratified by the Congress of the United
    States or January 1, 1971, whichever occurs
    earlier.
                    Explanatory Material:
     This Commission has negotiated an interstate compact
   with Nevada relative to the distribution and use of the
   waters of Lake Tahoe and the Truckee, Carson and
   Walker Rivers. Upon completion of ratification by the
   two states and the Congress, the Commission will have
   no further function. There is ample time between now
   and January 1, 1971, to accomplish these actions. There
   will be a resultant savings to the General F u n d of $15,-
   600.
   Statutes   Suspended:
        Chapter 2.6 (commencing with Section 8130) of Di-
        vision 1 of Title 2 of the Government Code
   Statutory   Amendments    and   Additions;
        None

12. The Goose Lake Compact Commission is elimi-
    nated effective when the compact has been rati-
    fied by the Congress of the United States or
    January 1, 1971, whichever occurs earlier.
                     Explanatory Material:
      This Commission has negotiated with a similar Oregon

13. The Governor's Council is eliminated.
                 Explanatory Material:
      The Governor's Council has grown so large and cum-
   bersome with its present membership of sixty-one that it
   is no longer an effective management tool.
      The Governor has established a working Cabinet which
   serves the purposes for which the Governor's Council was
   established many years ago. While there is no direct ap-
   propriation to the Council a great amount of valuable
   top-level time will be put to more productive use by elim-
   inating the Council.
   Statutes  Suspended:
        Government Code Sections 12040 and 12041
   Statutory Amendments    and    Additions:
        None

20. The Public Library Development Board is elimi-
    nated.
                 Explanatory Material:
      The Public Library Services Act, Chapter 1802, Statutes
   of 1963, provided for the improvement of locally financed
   free public libraries throughout the State by means of in-
   centive grants to public library systems. This is an annual
   grant of State funds of $800,000 at the present level. Ap-
   proximately three-quarters goes out to the local libraries on
   a per capita basis, and the remaining quarter is granted to
   help develop library systems. The program is administered
   by the State Librarian with the advice of this Board.
      I n the early stages of developing this program, it was
   valuable to have the Board to reconcile various conflicting
   interests. However, the program is now stabilized and
   three-quarters of the grant is on a fixed formula basis. The
   remainder can be administered by the State Librarian
   without the necessity for a statutory board. I n the event
   advice is needed it can be obtained on an ad hoc basis
   with no expense to the State.
      This Board has served its purpose and should be elimi-
   nated. There will be a resultant savings to the General
   F u n d of approximately $400 per year.
   Statutes Suspended:
        Education Code Sections 27115-27116.3
   Statutory Amendments    and    Additions:
        None

21. The Commission on IVIanpower, Automation and
    Technology is eliminated.
                  Explanatory Material:
      This Commission has been inactive and has received no
   funds in the last two years. In 1966-67 the Department
   of Employment Contingent F u n d provided $19,852 for the
                          - 1 6 -

   and Development Services Advisory Board cover the
   major areas of concern in the field formerly assigned to
   this Commission.
   Statutes Suspended:
        Division 1.5 (commencing with Section 160) of the
        Labor Code
   Statutory Amendments    and   Additions:
        None

   Statutory Amendments and Additions:
        Unemployment Insurance Code Section 10104

23. The Advisory Hospital Council is eliminated and
    its functions, authorities and responsibilities
    transferred to the Health Planning Council.
                  Explanatory Material:
      The Advisory Hospital Council has primary responsi-
   bility for allocation of Federal funds relative to hospital
   construction. The Health Planning Council was created
   to provide comprehensive State health planning in re-
   sponse to enactment of Public Law 89-749; its responsi-
   bilities are broader than those of the Advisory Hospital
   Council. There is thus some overlap and duplication of
                               — 17 —

    effort. The Health Planning Council can assume the func-
    tions of the Advisory Hospital Council and therefore the
    latter Council is no longer needed. There will be a result-
    ant savings to the General F u n d of $525.
    Statutes Suspended:
         Health and Safety Code Section 431.2
    Statutory Amendments and Additions:
         Health and Safety Code Section 431.6

24. The State Advisory Council (Department of Em-
    ployment) is eliminated and its functions, au-
    thorities and responsibilities transferred to the
    Job Training and Development Services Advisory
    Board.
                  Explanatory Material:
       This Council's function is to advise the Director of
    Employment on all matters pertaining to employment and
    unemployment. In conformity with Chapter 1460 of 1968,
    the Department of Employment will become part of the
    new Human Eesources Development Department at a
    date to be determined by the Administration but not
    later than January 1, 1970. The Job Training and De-
    velopment Services Advisory Board in the new depart-
    ment has functions parallel to those of the State Ad-
    visory Council. Therefore the Council is no longer
    needed because the Job Training and Development Serv-
    ices Advisory Board can assume its functions, and this
    will eliminate duplication of effort and possible conflicts.
    The Unemployment Administration F u n d provides $20,-
    046 and the Unemployment Compensation Disability F u n d
    $3,156 for support of this Council.
     Statutes   Suspended:
          Article 2 (commencing with Section 355) of Chapter
          2, Part 1, Division 1 of the Unemployment Insurance
          Code.
     Statutory Amendments and Additions:
          Unemployment Insurance Code Sections 10105, 10106,
          and 10107

25.* The Cannery Inspection Board is eliminated and
    its functions, authorities and responsibilities
    transferred to the Department of Public Health.
                    Explanatory Material:
      The function of this Board is to work with the Depart-
     ment of Public Health and the State Board of Public

* Superseded by legislative action. See Stats. 1969, Ch. 1031.
                          — 18 —
   Health in protecting the public with respect to canned
   foods. The Department and the State Board of Public
   Health can assume this responsibility without the need
   for a separate statutory board. If special expertise is
   needed, it can be obtained on an ad hoc basis at no ex-
   pense to the State.
   Statutes   Suspended:
        Article 2 (commencing with Section 28380) of Chap-
        ter 8 of Division 21 of the Health and Safety Code,
        and Health and Safety Code Sections 28401 and
        28441.
   Statutory Amendments and Additions:
        Health and Safety Code Sections 28380-28385, 28400,
        28402, 28403, and 28433

26. The Narcotic Rehabilitation Advisory Council is
    eliminated.
                 Explanatory Material:
      This Council's function is to act as an advisory group
   in matters of narcotic rehabilitation with special refer-
   ence to the California Kehabilitation Center. However,
   the new Inter-Agency Drug Abuse Council, formed under
   the auspices of the California Medical Association, can
   perform this function, and therefore the Narcotic Reha-
   bilitation Advisory Council is no longer necessary.
   Statutes   Suspended:
        "Welfare and Institutions Code Section 3004
   Statutory Amendments     and   Additions:
        None

27. The Coordinating Council on Alcohol Problems is
    eliminated.
                    Explanatory Material:
      This Council, consisting of directors of State depart-
   ments or other State agencies, is assigned to review, assess,
   and promote optional use of local, state and federal re-
   sources applicable to alcohol problems. The members are
   available on call as needed, coordination is provided
   through the Governor's Cabinet, and thus a formal statu-
   tory Council is not needed. The cost to the General Fund
   has been approximately $500 per year.
   Statutes Suspended:
        Health and Safety Code Section 427.8
   Statutory Amendments    and    Additions:
        None
                                — 19 —

28. The California Delinquency Prevention Commis-
    sion is eliminated and its functions, authorities
    and responsibilities transferred to the Governor's
    Advisory Committee on Children and Youth.
                        Explanatory Material:
        The function of this Commission is the prevention or
     reduction of delinquency among youths. The Governor's
     Advisory Committee on Children and Youth is concerned
     with all problems of children and youth and can assume
     the Commission's functions thereby removing the possi-
     bility of duplication and conflict.
        There will be a resultant savings to the General F u n d
     of $5,500.
     Statutes  Suspended:
          None
     Statutory Amendments and Additions:
          Welfare and Institutions Code Section 1752.5

29.* The New Car Dealers Policy and Appeals Board
    is eliminated.
                   Explanatory Material:
        This Board was established in 1967 by Chapter 1397.
     The functions of this Board are to prescribe rules and
     regulations relating to licensing of new car dealers, to
     hear and consider appeals from actions arising out of
     the decisions by the Department of Motor Vehicles, and
     to consider any matter concerning the activities or prac-
     tices of any person applying for or holding a license as
     a new car dealer pursuant to specified laws. Judicial re-
     views may be sought with respect to orders of this Board.
     The Board has met regularly during the past year and
     has not taken actions giving evidence of the need for
     continuance as a statutory formal State unit. Elimination
     of this Board will save the Department of Motor Vehicles
     $66,356.
     Statutes Suspended:
          Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 3000) of Di-
          vision 2 of the Vehicle Code and Vehicle Code Section
          11723
     Statutory Amendments        and     Additions:
          None




* Superseded by legislative action. See Stats. 1969, Ch. 1031.
                                 — 20 —
30.* The Marine Research Committee is eliminated
    and its functions, authorities and responsibilities
    transferred to the Fish and Game Commission.
                        Explanatory Material:
        The Fish and Game Commission can assume the respon-
     sibilities of this Committee and thus there is no need for
     continuing the Committee as a statutory entity.
     Statutes Suspended:
          Article 2 (commencing with Section 725) of Chapter
          1, Division 2 of the Fish and Game Code
     Statutory Amendments and Additions:
          Article 9 (commencing with Section 8085) is added to
          Chapter 1 of Part 3 of Division 6 of the Fish and
          Game Code and Section 222 of the Fish and Game
          Code

31. The Governor and Lieutenant Governor are re-
    moved from the California Toll Bridge Authority
    and replaced with two public members appointed
    at the pleasure of the Governor.
                       Explanatory Material:
       Attendance at the California Toll Bridge Authority
     meetings represent a time-consuming addition to the Gov-
     ernor's and Lieutenant Governor's duties, and, in many
     cases, such meetings are necessary only because of the for-
     malities required in bond proceedings. The proposed re-
     organization would relieve these constitutional officers of
     those duties while still retaining the stature of the Toll
     Bridge Authority as a responsible body with bonding pow-
     ers.
       There will be no resultant savings and no increase in
     operating costs.
     Statutes Suspended:
          None
     Statutory Amendments and Additions:
          Streets and Highways Code Section 30050




* Superseded by legislative action. See Stats. 1969, Ch. 1593.
                   GENERAL PROVISIONS
   This Eeorganizaion Plan is effective on the date specified by
Government Code Section 12080.5. The agencies, officers and
employees affected by this Plan shall continue to perform their
existing functions for sixty days following the effective date
of this Reorganization Plan and during this period shall plan
for the necessary changes. The reorganization changes herein
provided shall take place on the sixty-first day after the ef-
fective date of this Plan except as otherwise provided in this
Plan.
   In addition to the description of the reorganization of var-
ious agencies in the Executive Branch of the State Govern-
ment, there is also set forth explanatory material, the statutes
that are suspended (required by Government Code Sections
12080.2 and 12080.3(g)), and the statutes requiring amend-
ment. To facilitate understanding and reference, the explana-
tory material immediately follows the reorganization to which
it is applicable.
                   TRANSFER OF EMPLOYEES
   In accordance with Government Code Sections 12080.3 and
19370, all employees serving in the State civil service, other
than temporary employees, who are engaged in the perform-
ance of a function transferred to another agency, or engaged
in the administration of a law, the administration of which
is transferred to another agency by this Eeorganization Plan,
are transferred to the agency to which such function or ad-
ministration is transferred. The personnel records of all trans-
ferred employees shall be transferred to the agency to which
the employee is transferred. The status, positions, and rights
of such persons shall not be affected by their transfer and shall
continue to be retained by them pursuant to the State Civil
Service Act, except as to positions the duties of which are
vested in a position exempt from civil service. If any doubt
arises as to where such employees are transferred, the Person-
nel Board shall determine where an employee is transferred.
                      Explanatory Material:
    This provision is required by Government Code Section
    12080.3(c) and (d).


                             (21)
                          _   22 —

                    TRANSFER OF PROPERTY
   The property of any agency affected by this reorganization
is transferred to the agency to which the function or admin-
istration has been transferred. If any doubt arises as to where
such property is transferred, the Department of General
Services shall determine where the property is transferred.
The property of any agency which is abolished shall be trans-
ferred to the Department of General Services.
                       Explanatory Material:
     This provision is required by Government Code Section
     12080.3(d).
                     TRANSFER OF FUNDS
   All unexpended balances of appropriations and other funds
available for use in connection with any function or the ad-
ministration of any law transferred by this Reorganization
Plan shall be transferred to the agency to which the function
or administration has been transferred for use for the purpose
for which the appropriation was originally made or the funds
originally available. If there is any doubt as to where such
balances and funds are transferred, the Department of Fi-
nance shall determine where such balances and funds are
transferred. All unexpended balances of appropriations and
other funds for functions eliminated by this Reorganization
Plan shall revert to the fund from which appropriated as de-
termined by the Department of Finance.
                     Explanatory Material:
    This provision is required by Government Code Section
    12080.3(e).
            TERMINATION OF AGENCIES ABOLISHED
  The affairs of any agency abolished by this Reorganization
Plan shall be terminated as rapidly as possible. Such term-
ination shall be the responsibility of the Governor's Cabinet.
                     Explanatory Material:
    This provision is required by Government Code Section
    12080.3(f).

                          (3)
               GOVERNOR'S MESSAGE
   In accordance with Section 12080.2 of the Gov-
ernment Code, I am submitting Reorganization
Plan No. 2 of 1969 for review by the Legislature.
It is also being reviewed by the Commission on
California State Government Organization and
Economy. I have found each reorganization action
included in this Plan to be in the public interest.
   The actions proposed in this Plan will provide
a coordinated approach to harnessing and conserv-
ing the last great untapped resource of Califor-
nia—the ocean. This will assure the orderly
development and continuing administration of a
comprehensive coastal area plan to guide the many
decisions which affect the use of California's coast-
line.
   This is by no means all of the reorganizations I
am proposing. In my message of March 5, 1969, I
outlined this and several other major and necessary
changes. This Plan is an important element in the
continuing process of updating our State Govern-
ment.




                         (5)
                          — 7—

              REORGANIZATION ACTIONS
1. The Name of the Department of Harbors and Wa-
   teroraft is Changed to Department of Navigation
   and Ocean Development and Its Primary Emphasis
   Changed to Ocean-Oriented Activities.
                       Explanatory Material:
      Several agencies are now concerned with ocean-oriented
   activities without primary responsibility assigned to one
   department. The last great untapped resource available
   to the people of California is the ocean, and a coordinated
   effort is needed to explore the conservation and economic
   benefits available.
   Statutes  Suspended:
        None
   Statutory Amendments and Additions:
        Government Code Sections 11557 and 12805; Harbors
        and Navigation Code Sections 32, 33, 37, 50, 50.2, 80,
        85, 85.2, 651; Penal Code Section 830.4

2. The Name of the Harbors and Wateroraft Commis-
   sion Is Changed to Navigation and Ocean Develop-
   ment Commission and Membership Requirements
   Shall Be Based Solely on Geographic Representa-
   tion and Experience and Background Consistent
   With the Function of the Commission.
                     Explanatory Materials:
     This Commission will be advisory to the new Depart-
   ment of Navigation and Ocean Development and the name
   should reflect this. The primary requisite for membership
   should be geographical location as related to major ocean-
   ographic activities.
   Statutes Suspended :
        None
   Statutory Amendments and Additions :
        Harbors and Navigation Code Sections 31, 37, 50 2.
        80, 80.2, 80.4, 85.2, 651

3. The Boat Registration and Transfer Functions, Au-
   thorities and Responsibilities of the Department of
   Harbors and Wateroraft Are Transferred to the
   Department of Motor Vehicles.
                         _ 8 —

                     Explanatory Material:
      The Department of Motor Vehicles can handle the boat
   registration and transfer functions. Instantaneous infor-
   mation will be available to the new Department of Naviga-
   tion and Ocean Development. Only one central file in the
   Department of Motor Vehicles will be necessary.
   Statutes   Suspended:
        Article 2 (commencing with Section 680), Article 3
        (commencing with Section 700), Article 4 (commenc-
        ing with Section 750) of Chapter 5 of Division 3 of
        the Harbors and Navigation Code
   Statutory Amendments and Additions:
        Code of Civil Procedure Section 689(b), Uniform
        Commercial Code Sections 9302 and 10102, add Vehi-
        cle Code provisions incorporating the Articles listed
        above

4. The Boating Facility Planning and Design Func-
   tions, Authorities and Responsibilities of the De-
   partment of Parks and Recreation and the Office
   of Architecture and Construction are Transferred
   to the New Department of Navigation and Devel-
   opment.
                      Explanatory Material:
      Boating facility planning and design functions are now
   handled in the Department of Harbors and Watercraft,
   the Department of Parks and Eecreation and the Office
   of Architecture and Construction. This change will con-
   solidate these functions within one department with the
   primary responsibility for harbor planning and ocean
   resource development. This will be done without the
   necessity for additional funding.
   Statutes Suspended:
        None
   Statutory Amendments and Additions:
        Harbors and Navigation Code Section 85.2, Water
        Code Section 11910

5. The Beach Erosion Control Functions, Authorities
   and Responsibilities of the Department of Water
   Resources are Transferred to the New Department
   of Navigation and Ocean Development,
                                   — 9 —
                       Explanatory Material:
        An integral part of ocean resource planning is the
      control of beach erosion. As a state with the greatest
      beach resources in the world, California must have a co-
      ordinated approach to this problem. Placing this function
      in the new Department will provide such coordination.
      Statutes Suspended:
           Article 5 (commencing with Section 330) of Divi-
           sion 1 of Chapter 2.5 of the "Water Code
      Statutory Amendments and Additions:
           Add Harbors and Navigation Code provisions incor-
           porating the Article listed above

 6.* The Nonmineral Management Functions, Authori-
   ties and Responsibilities of All State Tidelands and
   Submerged Lands Lying Below Such Tidelands,
   and Swamp and Overflow Lands Affected by Tides,
   Including Any Such Lands Granted to a Local
   Agency, Currently Within the Jurisdiction of the
   State Lands Commission and the Division of State
   Lands Are Transferred to the New Department of
   Navigation and Ocean Development.
                        Explanatory Material:
        The management of tidelands and submerged lands
     lying below such tidelands are an integral part of man-
     aging the total coastal ocean environment. The new
     Department of Navigation and Ocean Development is the
     primary agency to coordinate all State ocean-oriented
     activities and thus is given the responsibility for tidelands
     and submerged lands lying below such tidelands. The
     responsibilities of other state agencies with regard to such
     lands remains unchanged except they have been asked to
     coordinate with the new Department of Navigation and
     Ocean Development.
     Statutes Suspended:
          Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 6301) of Part 1
          of Division 6 of the Public Eesources Code (to the
          extent relating to tidelands and submerged lands
          lying below such tidelands)
     Statutory Amendments and Additions:
          Public Eesources Code Sections within Chapters 3
          (commencing with Section 6201) and 4 (commencing
          with Section 6301) of P a r t 1, Chapter 1 (commencing
          with Section 6501) of P a r t 2, Article 9 (commenc-
